Variable Definition Node(k,i) Node above, upstream, and closest to the particle's position, defined as the upper-left node of the rectangular cell formed by intersection of vertical layer k and longitudinal segment i \(x_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\) Longitudinal position of Node(k,i) (m) \(\Delta x\) Offset (downstream) from Node(k,i) to the particle's position (m) \(z_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\) Vertical position of Node(k,i) (m) \(\Delta z\) Offset (below) from Node(k,i) to the particle's position (m) \(X^{t+1}\) Longitudinal position of particle at time \(t+1\) (m); defined as \(x_{\text{Node}(k,i)} + \Delta x\) at time \(t+1\) \(Z^{t+1}\) Vertical position of particle at time \(t+1\) (m); defined as \(z_{\text{Node}(k,i)} + \Delta z\) at time \(t+1\) \(X^{t}\) Longitudinal position of particle at time \(t\) (m); defined as \(x_{\text{Node}(k,i)} + \Delta x\) at time \(t\) \(Z^{t}\) Vertical position of particle at time \(t\) (m); defined as \(z_{\text{Node}(k,i)} + \Delta z\) at time \(t\) \(U^{t}(Z^{t}, X^{t})\) Interpolated horizontal flow velocity (m/s) at location \((Z^{t}, X^{t})\) \(W^{t}(Z^{t}, X^{t})\) Interpolated vertical flow velocity (m/s) at location \((Z^{t}, X^{t})\) \(\Delta t\) Time interval between time \(t\) and time \(t+1\) (seconds) Figure 44. From Goodwin et al. (2001) illustrating the particle transport through the CE-QUAL-W2 grid.

docs.title: Boundary Checks
docs.text:
After \(X^{t+1}\) and \(Z^{t+1}\) are calculated, boundary checks are performed to determine if the particle's new position exceeds either the longitudinal or vertical boundaries of the cell containing \(X^{t}\) and \(Z^{t}\), or any system boundary. An algorithm is activated to determine the appropriate cell in which to place the particle if the particle's new position exceeds the boundaries of its cell from the previous time step. Once the appropriate cell is found, the values of k, i, Node(k,i), \(x_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\), \(z_{\text{Node}(k,i)}\), \(\Delta x\), and \(\Delta z\) are updated for the particle at \(t+1\) and stored.

Since the displacement of a particle is proportional to the time step used, the displacement calculated in Equations 3-1 and/or 3-2 could position the particle outside system boundaries. To correct for this, the model places a particle near the boundary at a user-specified distance if \(X^{t+1}\) or \(Z^{t+1}\) exceeds the system boundaries.

docs.title: Turbulent Diffusion
docs.text:
In addition, a random movement of the particle is added to the velocity movement. The randomness added to the particle movement is based on the intensity of turbulence in a system. Following the work of Dunsbergen and Stalling (1993) and Chapman et al. (1994), the transport in x and z including the translation by velocity and random turbulent transport are shown below:

\[ X^{t+1} = X^{t} + U \Delta t + R\sqrt{6 D_x \Delta t} \tag{3-3} \] \[ Z^{t+1} = Z^{t} + W \Delta t + R\sqrt{6 D_z \Delta t} \tag{3-4} \]

where:

  • \(R\) = a random number having a uniform distribution with zero mean and unit variance
  • \(D_x\) = longitudinal mass/heat dispersion coefficient
  • \(D_z\) = vertical mass/heat dispersion coefficient

The use of the uniform distribution rather than a Gaussian distribution saves computational time and does not affect the resulting random distribution (Hathhorn, 1997).

docs.title: Dispersion Coefficient Specification
docs.text:
The value of \(D_x\) is specified in the control file w2_con.npt, whereas the value of \(D_z\) is computed based on the turbulence closure model used, such as the k-ε turbulence model (for example in w2_con.npt the user can set AZC=TKE). The choice of \(D_x\) can lead to high values of random movement in x if \(D_x\) is high. In all cases the maximum movement of a particle is constrained by the grid cell height, \(\Delta z\), and segment length, \(\Delta x\).

High Dispersion Coefficient Values

Setting \(D_x\) to a high value can cause excessive random movement of particles. The maximum particle movement per time step is bounded by the grid cell dimensions (\(\Delta z\) and \(\Delta x\)).

docs.title: Lateral Transport
docs.text:
Particles also move in the lateral direction based on the following equation, assuming that the lateral dispersion coefficient is the same as the longitudinal coefficient:

\[ Y^{t+1} = Y^{t} + V \Delta t + R\sqrt{6 D_x \Delta t} \tag{3-5} \]

The value of \(V\) is based on any lateral inflows or outflows at a segment.

docs.title: Particle Location in the Grid
docs.text: The location of the particles in the grid is identified by segment (I) and layer (K) location as well as X, Y, and Z coordinates within each layer. Figure 45 and Figure 46 show the x, y, and z coordinate reference locations within the cells for the particle algorithm for the plan view and side view, respectively. Figure 47 shows the definition sketch for lateral velocities in a layer. The standard CE-QUAL-W2 designation for longitudinal (positive downstream or increasing segment number) and vertical velocities (positive downward) is followed in this algorithm. Initial x, y, and z are given for each particle released into a segment and layer. The user specifies x and z, but y is chosen as the middle of a layer, i.e., \(y = B/2\) where \(B\) is the layer width.

docs.title: Plan View Coordinates
docs.text:
Figure 45. Plan view of x and y coordinates within a layer (K) and segment (I). DLX is the segment length and B is the segment width at the given layer K.

Within a given layer K and segment I, the coordinate system for the plan view is defined as follows:

  • X-coordinate: Ranges from 0 at the right (looking downstream) to DLX at the left, with DLX\(/2\) at the center.
  • Y-coordinate: Ranges from 0 at the left bank (looking upstream) to \(B\) at the right bank, with \(B/2\) at the center.

docs.title: Side View Coordinates
docs.text:
Figure 46. Side view of z and y coordinates within a layer (K) and segment (I). DZ is the layer thickness and B is the layer width.

Within a given layer K and segment I, the coordinate system for the side view is defined as follows:

  • Z-coordinate: Ranges from 0 at the top of the layer to DZ at the bottom, with DZ\(/2\) at the midpoint.
  • Y-coordinate: Same convention as the plan view (0 to \(B\)).

docs.title: Lateral and Longitudinal Velocities
docs.text:
Figure 47. Definition sketch for lateral and longitudinal velocities within the cells. Withdrawals are always assumed to be on the LHS (left-hand side) of the segment.

The velocity sign conventions within each cell are:

  • Longitudinal velocity: Positive in the downstream direction (toward segment I+1), negative in the upstream direction.
  • Lateral velocity: Positive to the right (looking downstream), negative to the left.
  • Withdrawals: Always assumed to be on the left-hand side (LHS) of the segment.
  • Side branches: Can connect on either the left-hand side (LHS) or right-hand side (RHS) of a segment.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapman, R.S., Johnson, B.H., and Vemulakonda, S.R. (1994). User's Guide for the Sigma Stretched Version of CH3D-WES; a Three-Dimensional Numerical Hydrodynamic, Salinity, and Temperature Model. Technical Report HL-96-21, U.S. Army Engineer Waterways Experiment Station, Vicksburg, MS.
  • Dunsbergen, D.W., and Stalling, G.S. (1993). The Application of a Particle Model to Coastal and Estuarine Problems. Delft University of Technology, Dept. of Civil Engineering, Delft, The Netherlands.
  • Goodwin, R.A., Nestler, J.M., Anderson, J.J., Weber, L.J., and Loucks, D.P. (2001). A New Tool to Forecast Fish Movement and Passage. Hydro Review, 25(4), 74--82.
  • Hathhorn, W.E. (1997). A Second Look at the Method of Random Walks. Stochastic Hydrology and Hydraulics, 11(4), 319--329.

docs.title: Temperature and Water Quality Modeling
docs.text: This chapter describes the theoretical basis for temperature and water quality modeling in CE-QUAL-W2. The model simulates temperature and an arbitrary number of water quality constituents using the turbulent advection-diffusion equation. Each constituent is subject to lateral and vertical transport as well as kinetic source and sink terms that represent biological, chemical, and physical transformations.

docs.title: Temperature and Water Quality Transport
docs.text:
The instantaneous velocity and concentration are decomposed into a mean and an unsteady component (Figure 49):

Figure 49. Concentration variability with time. \[ \bar{u} = \frac{1}{T}\int_t^{t+T} u(t)\, dt \tag{4-1} \]

Similarly for w, v, and c:

\[ v = \bar{v} + v', \quad w = \bar{w} + w', \quad c = \bar{c} + c' \tag{4-2} \]

Substituting these into the 3D governing equation and time averaging:

\[ \frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial t} + \bar{u}\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial x} + \bar{v}\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial y} + \bar{w}\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial z} = D\left[\frac{\partial^2 \bar{c}}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \bar{c}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \bar{c}}{\partial z^2}\right] - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\overline{u'c'}) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\overline{v'c'}) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(\overline{w'c'}) + \bar{S} \tag{4-3} \]

The new terms in the governing equation represent mass transport by turbulent eddies. As the intensity of turbulence increases, turbulent mass transport increases. The turbulent mass fluxes are defined as:

\[ \bar{J}_t = \left(\overline{u'c'}, \overline{v'c'}, \overline{w'c'}\right) \tag{4-4} \]

Using the gradient-diffusion (Fickian) approximation:

\[ \overline{u'c'} = -E_x\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial x}, \quad \overline{v'c'} = -E_y\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial y}, \quad \overline{w'c'} = -E_z\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial z} \]

Substituting into the governing equation:

\[ \frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial t} + \bar{u}\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial x} + \bar{v}\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial y} + \bar{w}\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[(E_x + D)\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial x}\right] + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left[(E_y + D)\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial y}\right] + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left[(E_z + D)\frac{\partial \bar{c}}{\partial z}\right] + \bar{S} \tag{4-5} \]

In turbulent fluids, \(E_x\), \(E_y\), and \(E_z\) >> \(D\), and \(D\) can be neglected except at interfaces where turbulence goes to zero. The turbulent diffusion coefficients can be thought of as the product of the velocity scale of turbulence and the length scale of that turbulence. These coefficients are related to the turbulent eddy viscosity. In general, these turbulent diffusion coefficients are non-isotropic and non-homogeneous.

Spatial averages across the lateral dimension of the channel of the turbulent time-averaged quantities can now be introduced:

\[ \overline{\bar{c}} = \overline{\bar{c}} + c'', \quad \overline{\bar{u}} = \overline{\bar{u}} + u'', \quad \overline{\bar{w}} = \overline{\bar{w}} + w'' \tag{4-6} \]

where the double overbar is a spatial average over y and the double prime is the deviation from the spatial mean. Figures 50 and 51 illustrate the lateral average of the velocity and concentration fields, respectively.

Figure 50. Lateral average of the velocity field. Figure 51. Lateral average of the concentration field.

These are substituted into the governing equation and integrated over the width such that:

\[ \frac{\partial B\tilde{c}}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial B\tilde{u}\tilde{c}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial B\tilde{w}\tilde{c}}{\partial z} = -B\left(\tilde{v}\tilde{c}|_{y2} - \tilde{v}\tilde{c}|_{y1} + \overline{c'v'}|_{y2} - \overline{c'v'}|_{y1}\right) \] \[ + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left((D + E_x)B\frac{\partial \tilde{c}}{\partial x}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left((D + E_z)B\frac{\partial \tilde{c}}{\partial z}\right) - \left[\frac{\partial B\overline{u''c''}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial B\overline{w''c''}}{\partial z}\right] + \bar{r}B \tag{4-7} \]

The terms are simplified as follows:

\[ \frac{1}{B}\int_{y1}^{y2}\frac{\partial(\tilde{c}+c'')}{\partial t}\,dy = \frac{1}{B}\int_{y1}^{y2}\frac{\partial(\tilde{c})}{\partial t}\,dy + \frac{1}{B}\int_{y1}^{y2}\frac{\partial(c'')}{\partial t}\,dy \] \[ = \frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{y1}^{y2}\tilde{c}\,dy + \frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{y1}^{y2}c''\,dy = \frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial B\tilde{c}}{\partial t} \tag{4-8} \] \[ \frac{1}{B}\int_{y1}^{y2}\frac{\partial(\tilde{u}+u'')(\tilde{c}+c'')}{\partial x}\,dy = \frac{1}{B}\int_{y1}^{y2}\frac{\partial(\tilde{c}\tilde{u})}{\partial x}\,dy + \frac{1}{B}\int_{y1}^{y2}\frac{\partial(c''u'')}{\partial t}\,dy \] \[ = \frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\int_{y1}^{y2}\tilde{c}\tilde{u}\,dy + \frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\int_{y1}^{y2}c''u''\,dy = \frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial B\tilde{u}\tilde{c}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial B\overline{u''c''}}{\partial x} \tag{4-9} \]

The spatial average of any double primed variable goes to zero by definition. The turbulent dispersion coefficients are defined as:

\[ \overline{u''c''} = -D_x\frac{\partial \overline{\tilde{c}}}{\partial x} \tag{4-10} \] \[ \overline{w''c''} = -D_z\frac{\partial \overline{\tilde{c}}}{\partial z} \]

The dispersion terms are a result of lateral averaging of the velocity field. In general, except at an interface, \(D_x\) >> \(E_x\) >> \(D\) and similarly for \(D_z\) >> \(E_z\) >> \(D\). Substituting the dispersion coefficients and using \(q\) to be the net mass transport from lateral boundaries, the equation becomes:

\[ \frac{\partial B\tilde{c}}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial B\overline{\tilde{u}}\tilde{c}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial B\overline{\tilde{w}}\tilde{c}}{\partial z} = qB + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(D_xB\frac{\partial \tilde{c}}{\partial x}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(D_zB\frac{\partial \tilde{c}}{\partial z}\right) + \bar{r}B \tag{4-11} \]

If the overbars are dropped and replaced with capitals, c is replaced with \(\Phi\), then the following equation is obtained:

\[ \frac{\partial B\Phi}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial UB\Phi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WB\Phi}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[BD_x\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x}\right] - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left[BD_z\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial z}\right] = q_\Phi B + S_\Phi B \tag{4-12} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi\) = laterally averaged constituent concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(D_x\) = longitudinal temperature and constituent dispersion coefficient, m² s⁻¹
  • \(D_z\) = vertical temperature and constituent dispersion coefficient, m² s⁻¹
  • \(q_\Phi\) = lateral inflow or outflow mass flow rate of constituent per unit volume, g m⁻³ s⁻¹
  • \(S_\Phi\) = laterally averaged source/sink term, g m⁻³ s⁻¹

Note that this can be concentration or temperature since the concentration of heat can be determined to be \(\rho c_p T\) where \(\rho\) is the fluid density, \(c_p\) is the specific heat of water, and T is the temperature. In this case the source-sink term for temperature would be \(S_T = -\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z}\) where \(\varphi\) is the heat flux in units of W m⁻².

The following must be known in order to solve the equation:

  1. Laterally averaged velocity field from the momentum equations
  2. Appropriate boundary and initial conditions
  3. \(D_x\) and \(D_z\)
  4. Laterally averaged source/sink terms

docs.title: Determination of \(D_z\) and \(D_x\)
docs.text:
The specification of \(D_x\), the longitudinal dispersion coefficient, is a user-defined input. The preprocessor does a check on the magnitude of this value by computing \(D_x\) based on an approach by Okubo (1971):

\[ D_x = 5.84 \times 10^{-4} \Delta x^{1.1} \]

where \(D_x\) is in m²/s and the longitudinal grid spacing \(\Delta x\) is in m. \(D_x\) can also be set to be a function of the mean velocity or this value can be space and time invariant. \(D_x\) can be computed dynamically using:

\[ D_x = \beta \overline{\overline{U}} \Delta z \]

where \(\beta\) is a user input value and \(\overline{\overline{U}}\) is the time-averaged, laterally averaged longitudinal velocity at a segment and layer. Hence, the dispersion coefficient scales with the average longitudinal velocity.

\(D_z\) is internally computed within the CE-QUAL-W2 model using the Reynolds analogy, where \(D_z\) is computed from \(A_z\), the vertical eddy viscosity, from:

\[ D_z = 0.14 A_z \]

docs.title: Surface Heat Exchange
docs.text:
The surface heat exchange is treated as a flux boundary condition at the water surface. Surface heat exchange can be formulated as a term-by-term process (see Figure 52) using the explicit adjacent cell transport computation as long as the integration timestep is shorter than or equal to the frequency of the meteorological input. Surface heat exchange processes depending on water surface temperatures are computed using computations from the prior time step.

Figure 52. Surface heat exchange term-by-term formulation.

Term-by-term surface heat exchange is computed as:

\[ \Phi_n = \Phi_s - \Phi_{sr} + \Phi_a - \Phi_{ar} - \Phi_{br} - \Phi_e - \Phi_c \tag{4-13} \]

where:

  • \(\phi_n\) = net surface heat flux, W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_s\) = incoming short-wave solar radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_{sr}\) = reflected short-wave solar radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_{sn}\) = net short-wave solar radiation, \(\phi_s - \phi_{sr}\), W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_a\) = incoming long-wave atmospheric radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_{ar}\) = reflected atmospheric long-wave radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_{br}\) = back long-wave radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_e\) = evaporative heat loss, W m⁻²
  • \(\phi_c\) = conductive heat loss, W m⁻²

The short-wave solar radiation is either measured directly or computed from sun angle relationships and cloud cover. Annear and Wells (2007) provide an overview of formulae for short-wave solar radiation. If the model user chooses the internally computed short-wave solar, the model computes the net clear sky solar radiation \(\phi_s\) (net short-wave solar radiation in Btu/ft²/day) using the EPA (1971) relationship:

\[ \phi_s = 24(2.044A_o + 0.1296A_o^2 - 1.941E - 3A_o^3 + 7.591E - 6A_o^4) \times 0.1314 \tag{4-14} \]

Note that this equation includes the average reflection loss of short-wave solar radiation. The solar altitude \(A_o\) (degrees) is calculated from Equation 4-15. Cloud cover reduction of clear sky solar radiation uses the relationship (Wunderlich, 1972): \(\phi_{s,net} = \phi_{s,clearsky}(1 - 0.65C^2)\) where C is the cloud cover fraction between 0 and 1.

The long-wave atmospheric radiation, \(\phi_a\), is computed from air temperature and cloud cover using Brunt's formula (Figure 53): \(\varphi_a = \varepsilon\sigma T^{*4}\) where \(\varepsilon\) is the average emittance of atmosphere, \(\sigma\) is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.62 x 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² °K⁻⁴), and \(T^*\) is air temperature in absolute scale (°K). The model uses the clear sky formulae of Swinbank (1963): \(\varphi_{ac} = 5.31 \times 10^{-13}(T_a + 273)^6\). Below 5 °C the formula of Idso and Jackson (1969) is used: \(\varphi_{ac} = \sigma(T_a + 273)^4(1 - 0.261\exp[-7.77 \times 10^{-4}T_a^2])\). The effect of clouds is: \(\phi_a = \phi_{ac}(1 + kC^2)\) where k = 0.17 (average). The reflection is assumed to be 3%, i.e., \(\phi_{an} = 0.97\phi_a\).

Figure 53. Difference in incoming long-wave atmospheric radiation formulae between Swinbank and Idso and Jackson.

Water surface back radiation is computed as:

\[ \phi_{br} = \varepsilon\sigma(T_s + 273.15)^4 \tag{4-24} \]

where \(\varepsilon\) = emissivity of water (0.97), \(\sigma\) = Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67 x 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² °K⁻⁴), and \(T_s\) = water surface temperature (°C).

Evaporative heat loss is computed as:

\[ \phi_e = f(W_z)(e_s - e_a) \tag{4-25} \]

where \(f(W_z)\) is the evaporative wind speed function (W m⁻² mmHg⁻¹), \(e_s\) is saturation vapor pressure at the water surface (mmHg), and \(e_a\) is atmospheric vapor pressure (mmHg).

Surface heat conduction is computed as:

\[ \phi_c = C_c f(W_z)(T_s - T_a) \tag{4-26} \]

where \(C_c\) = Bowen's coefficient (0.47 mmHg °C⁻¹) and \(T_a\) = air temperature (°C).

Short-wave solar radiation penetrates the surface and decays exponentially with depth according to Beer's Law (see Figure 54):

\[ \phi_s(z) = (1 - \beta)\phi_{sn}e^{-\eta z} \tag{4-27} \]

where \(\phi_s(z)\) = short-wave radiation at depth z (W m⁻²), \(\beta\) = fraction absorbed at the water surface, \(\eta\) = extinction coefficient (m⁻¹), and \(\phi_{sn}\) = net short-wave solar radiation reaching the surface (W m⁻²).

Figure 54. Short-wave solar penetration in a water body.

docs.title: Evaporation Models for f(W)
docs.text:
The evaporative wind speed function, \(f(W_z)\), chosen by the model user can affect surface temperatures especially in the summer. Various formulations of \(f(W_z)\) have been catalogued and examined in Edinger et al. (1974). The model user can include different evaporation formulations using:

\[ f(W_z) = a + bW_z^c \tag{4-28} \]

where \(a\) = 9.2 (default), \(b\) = 0.46 (default), \(c\) = 2 (default), and \(W_z\) = wind speed measured at 2 m (m s⁻¹). The wind height conversion uses:

\[ b_{2m} = \alpha^c b_z \tag{4-29} \] \[ \frac{W_{2m}}{W_z} = \frac{\ln(2/z_0)}{\ln(z/z_0)} = \frac{1}{\alpha} \tag{4-30} \]

where \(z_0\) = wind roughness height. Typical roughness values: 0.001 m for wind < 2.3 m/s and 0.005 m for wind > 2.3 m/s. The Ryan-Harleman (1974) formulation is: \(f(W_z) = a + bW_z\) (Eq. 4-31). A comparison of wind speed formulations is shown in Figure 55 where \(b\) = 4.1 W m⁻² mmHg⁻¹ m⁻¹ s⁻¹, \(a = \lambda(T_v - T_{av})^{1/3}\), and \(\lambda\) = 3.59 W m² mmHg °C⁻¹/³. For Lake Hefner, \(a\) = 0 and \(b\) = 4.99.

Figure 55. Comparison of the wind speed formulation for Ryan-Harleman and W2 default (for Tair=15 °C, Tdew=-5 °C, Tsurface=25 °C).

docs.title: Equilibrium Temperature
docs.text:
The equilibrium temperature, \(T_E\), is defined as the temperature at which the net rate of surface heat exchange is zero (see Figure 56).

Figure 56. Concept of the equilibrium temperature, TE, where the net surface heat flux is defined as zero.

The net rate of surface heat exchange is expressed as:

\[ \phi_n = -K(T_s - T_E) \tag{4-32} \]

where:

  • \(\phi_n\) = net rate of surface heat exchange, W m⁻²
  • \(K\) = coefficient of surface heat exchange, W m⁻² °C⁻¹
  • \(T_s\) = water surface temperature, °C
  • \(T_E\) = equilibrium temperature, °C

Seven separate heat exchange processes are summarized in the coefficient of surface heat exchange and equilibrium temperature. The linearization is examined in detail by Brady, et al. (1969) and Edinger et al. (1974). \(T_E\) can be computed from the heat flux equation where \(\phi_n\) = 0 or using the approximate technique (Brady et al., 1969). \(K\) can be computed from the slope of net flux vs temperature or using the approximate formula (Brady et al., 1969): \(K = 23 + (\beta_w + 0.255)17W_2\) where \(\beta_w = 0.255 - 0.0085T_w + 0.000204T_w^2\).

docs.title: Sediment Heat Exchange
docs.text:
Sediment heat exchange with water is generally small compared to surface heat exchange and many previous modelers have neglected it. Investigations on several reservoirs have shown the process must be included to accurately reproduce hypolimnetic temperatures. The formulation is similar to surface heat exchange:

\[ H_{sw} = -K_{sw}(T_w - T_s) \tag{4-33} \]

where:

  • \(H_{sw}\) = rate of sediment/water heat exchange, W m⁻²
  • \(K_{sw}\) = coefficient of sediment/water heat exchange, W m⁻² °C⁻¹
  • \(T_w\) = water temperature, °C
  • \(T_s\) = sediment temperature, °C

The sediment heat exchange process is illustrated in Figure 57. The variable \(K_{sw}\) is defined as \(\left[\frac{\rho c_p D}{L}\right]\) where D is the diffusion coefficient, \(\rho\) is the density, \(c_p\) is the coefficient of specific heat, and L is a length scale (typically the distance between the water cell center and sediment cell layer).

Figure 57. Schematic of sediment heat exchange.

Previous applications used a value of 0.3 W m⁻² °C⁻¹ for \(K_{sw}\). Average yearly air temperature has been used as an estimate of \(T_s\) (Todd, 1980). The default model value shown in Part 3 was 0.3 W m⁻² °C⁻¹.

docs.title: Solar Altitude and Azimuth
docs.text:
The solar altitude and azimuth geometry is shown in Figure 58. The declination angle, \(\delta\), is computed from Spencer (1971) using Equation 4-34 (same form as Eq. 4-21). The local hour is \(HOUR = 24(JD_r - JD_i)\) (Eq. 4-35). The equation of time correction is \(EQT = 0.17\sin\frac{4\pi(JD_i - 80)}{373} - 0.129\sin\frac{2\pi(JD_i - 8)}{355}\) (Eq. 4-36). The local hour angle is:

\[ H = \frac{2\pi}{24}\left[HOUR + (Long - \varphi)\frac{24}{360} + EQT - 12\right] \tag{4-37} \] Figure 58. Schematic of solar altitude, Ao, and azimuth, Az.

The solar altitude, \(A_o\), is calculated from Wunderlich (1972):

\[ A_o = A\sin\left[\sin\left(lat \times \frac{\pi}{180}\right)\sin(\delta) + \cos\left(lat \times \frac{\pi}{180}\right)\cos(\delta)\cos(H)\right] \tag{4-38} \]

The solar azimuth is computed as (Nautical Almanac, 2001):

\[ X = \frac{\sin(\delta)\cos\left(\frac{Lat \cdot \pi}{180}\right) - \cos(\delta)\cos(H)\sin\left(\frac{Lat \cdot \pi}{180}\right)}{\cos A_o} \tag{4-39} \]

If \(X > 1\), \(X = 1\); if \(X < -1\), \(X = -1\) (Eq. 4-40). Then \(A = A\cos X\) (Eq. 4-41) and \(AZ = 2\pi - A\); if \(H < 0\), \(AZ = A\) (Eq. 4-42). Figure 59 illustrates the relationship between topographic and vegetative shading and solar altitude.

Figure 59. Schematic of topographic and vegetative shading, solar altitude (αo), and vegetation height (T) and their effect on shadow length.

docs.title: Topographic Shading
docs.text: The algorithm uses the position of the sun to determine which topographic inclination angle coincides with the direction of incoming solar radiation. The algorithm determines the closest two inclination angles and linearly interpolates for the specific solar direction. If the solar altitude is below the calculated topographic inclination angle, then topographic shading dominates and the short-wave solar radiation is reduced by 90% for complete shade. This allows for 10% of the incoming solar radiation as diffuse radiation even when in the shade.

docs.title: Vegetative Shading
docs.text:
If the topographic angle is less than the solar altitude, vegetative shade dominates. The tree shadow length, \(S_T\), is calculated as:

\[ S_T = \frac{T}{\tan A_0} \tag{4-43} \] \[ S_W = S_T - \frac{E}{\sin(\theta_0 - \alpha_A)} \tag{4-44} \] \[ S_N = S_W\sin(\theta_0 - \alpha_A) \tag{4-45} \]

Simplifying: \(S_N = \frac{T \times \sin(\theta_0 - \alpha_A)}{\tan A_0} - E\) (Eq. 4-46). The shade factor is:

\[ sfact = SRF\frac{S_N}{B} \tag{4-47} \] \[ Shade = (1 - sfact) \tag{4-48} \] \[ SRO_{net} = SRO \times Shade \tag{4-49} \]

The azimuth angle and stream orientation are shown in Figures 60 and 61.

Figure 60. Azimuth angle, αA, and stream orientation, Θo. Figure 61. Relationship between azimuth, stream orientation, and shadow length.

docs.title: Data Requirements
docs.text:
The shade algorithm reads in 18 topographic inclination angles surrounding each segment center-point. The first inclination angle is taken from directly North of a segment (orientation angle 0.0) and moves clockwise to the East with increasing orientation angles in 20° increments. The user can specify dynamic shading reduction factors as a function of time for leaf growth and fall for deciduous trees.

Table 8. Criteria for determining sunward bank

Sunward Bank \(0° < \theta_0 \leq 180°\) \(180° < \theta_0 \leq 360°\) Left \(\alpha_A < \theta_0\) or \(\alpha_A > \theta_0 + 180°\) \(\theta_0 - 180° < \alpha_A < \theta_0\) Right \(\theta_0 < \alpha_A < \theta_0 + 180°\) \(\alpha_A > \theta_0\) or \(\alpha_A < \theta_0 - 180°\)

Dynamic shading requires segment-specific data including:

  • Topographic shade angles (18 per segment)
  • Vegetation characteristics: tree height, crown width, distance from bank, and canopy density
  • Model segment orientation (azimuth)

These data are specified in the shade input file.

docs.title: Ice Cover
docs.text:
Ice thickness, onset, and loss of ice cover play an important role in the heat budget of northern waterbodies. At high latitudes, ice cover may remain until late spring or early summer and prevent warming due to absorption of short-wave solar radiation.

The ice model is based on an ice cover with ice-to-air heat exchange, conduction through the ice, conduction between underlying water, and a "melt temperature" layer on the ice bottom (Ashton, 1979). The overall heat balance for the water-to-ice-to-air system is:

\[ \rho_i L_f \frac{\Delta h}{\Delta t} = h_{ai}(T_i - T_e) - h_{wi}(T_w - T_m) \tag{4-50} \]

where:

  • \(\rho_i\) = density of ice, kg m⁻³
  • \(L_f\) = latent heat of fusion of ice, J kg⁻¹
  • \(\Delta h/\Delta t\) = change in ice thickness (h) with time (t), m s⁻¹
  • \(h_{ai}\) = coefficient of ice-to-air heat exchange, W m⁻² °C⁻¹
  • \(h_{wi}\) = coefficient of water-to-ice heat exchange through the melt layer, W m⁻² °C⁻¹
  • \(T_i\) = ice temperature, °C
  • \(T_e\) = equilibrium temperature of ice-to-air heat exchange, °C
  • \(T_w\) = water temperature below ice, °C
  • \(T_m\) = melt temperature, 0 °C

Ice temperature in the ice-heat balance is computed by equating the rate of surface heat transfer between ice and air to the rate of heat conduction through ice:

\[ h_{ai}(T_i - T_{ei}) = \frac{-k_i(T_i - T_m)}{h} \tag{4-51} \]

where \(k_i\) = molecular heat conductivity of ice, W m⁻¹ °C⁻¹.

When solved for ice temperature, \(T_i\), and inserted in the overall ice-heat balance, the ice thickness relationship becomes:

\[ \rho_i L_f \frac{\Delta h}{\Delta t} = \frac{(T_M - T_{ei})}{\frac{h}{k_i} + \frac{1}{h_{ia}}} - h_{wi}(T_w - T_m) \tag{4-52} \]

docs.title: Initial Ice Formation
docs.text:
Formation of ice requires lowering the surface water temperature to the freezing point by normal surface heat exchange processes. The negative water surface temperature is then converted to equivalent ice thickness:

\[ \theta_0 = \frac{-T_{wn}\rho_w C_{P_w} h}{\rho_i L_f} \tag{4-53} \]

where:

  • \(\theta_0\) = thickness of initial ice formation during a timestep, m
  • \(T_{wn}\) = local temporary negative water temperature, °C
  • \(h\) = layer thickness, m
  • \(\rho_w\) = density of water, kg m⁻³
  • \(C_{P_w}\) = specific heat of water, J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹
  • \(\rho_i\) = density of ice, kg m⁻³
  • \(L_f\) = latent heat of fusion, J kg⁻¹

docs.title: Air-Ice Flux Boundary Condition and Ice Surface Temperature Approximation
docs.text:
The ice surface temperature, \(T_s\), must be known to calculate the heat components, \(H_{br}\), \(H_e\), \(H_c\), and the thermal gradient in the ice. The approximate value for \(T_s\) is obtained by linearizing the ice thickness across the timestep and solving for \(T_s\):

\[ T_s^n \approx \frac{\theta^{n-1}}{K_i}[H_{sn}^n + H_{an}^n - H_{br}(T_s^n) - H_e(T_s^n) - H_c(T_s^n)] \tag{4-54} \]

The heat flux through the ice is:

\[ q_i = K_i\frac{T_f - T_s(t)}{\theta(t)} \tag{4-56} \]

where \(K_i\) = thermal conductivity of ice (W m⁻¹ °C⁻¹), \(T_f\) = freezing point temperature (°C), and \(\theta\) = thickness of ice (m).

docs.title: Absorbed Solar Radiation by Water Under Ice
docs.text:
The amount of solar radiation absorbed by water under the ice cover may be expressed as:

\[ H_{ps} = H_s(1 - ALB)(1 - \beta_i)e^{-\gamma_i\theta(t)} \tag{4-57} \]

where:

  • \(H_{ps}\) = solar radiation absorbed by water under ice cover, W m⁻²
  • \(H_s\) = incident solar radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(ALB_i\) = ice albedo
  • \(\beta_i\) = fraction of the incoming solar radiation absorbed in the ice surface
  • \(\gamma_i\) = ice extinction coefficient, m⁻¹

docs.title: Ice Melt at Air-Ice Interface
docs.text:
Stored energy used for melting ice is expressed as:

\[ \rho_i C_{p_i}\frac{T_s(t)}{2}\theta(t) = \rho_i L_f \Delta\theta_{ai} \tag{4-58} \]

where \(C_{pi}\) = specific heat of ice (J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹) and \(\theta_{ai}\) = ice melt at the air-ice interface (m⁻¹).

docs.title: Ice-Water Flux Boundary Condition
docs.text:
Both ice growth and melt may occur at the ice-water interface. An imbalance between the fluxes provides a mechanism for freezing or melting:

\[ q_i - q_{iw} = \rho_i L_f \frac{d\theta_{iw}}{dt} \tag{4-59} \]

The heat flux at the ice-water interface is:

\[ q_{iw} = h_{wi}(T_w(t) - T_f) \tag{4-60} \]

Ice growth or melt at the ice-water interface is:

\[ \Delta\theta_{iw}^n = \frac{1}{\rho_i L_f}\left[K_i\frac{T_f - T_s^n}{\theta^{n-1}} - h_{wi}(T_w^n - T_f)\right] \tag{4-61} \]

docs.title: Freezing Temperature of Ice
docs.text:
In general, the temperature at which water freezes, \(T_f\), is set to 0 °C for fresh water. If the model is set to SALT (see WTYPEC input), the freezing temperature is affected by the salinity. For TDS < 35 ppt:

\[ T_f = -0.0545 TDS \tag{4-62} \]

For TDS > 35 ppt:

\[ T_f = -0.3146 - 0.0417 TDS - 0.000166 TDS^2 \tag{4-63} \]

docs.title: Gain and Loss of Water
docs.text:
As ice forms, water is removed from the waterbody (Figure 62). There is a removal of 0.917 m³ of water for every 1 m³ of ice formed. The reverse occurs as ice melts and comes back into the water body. The model does not account for ablation nor on snow accumulation.

Figure 62. Ice formation and melting water balance.

docs.title: Overview of Kinetic Source/Sink Term
docs.text:
In order to solve the 2D advection-diffusion equation, the source/sink term, \(S_\Phi\), must be specified. The model solves for temperature and a user-specified number of water quality variables. Water quality state variables along with their kinetic source/sink terms are shown in Table 9. The user can specify any number of generic constituents [NGC], suspended solids groups [NSS], CBOD groups [NBOD], algal groups [NAL], macrophyte groups [NMC], zooplankton groups [NZP], and periphyton/epiphyton groups [NEP].
