In addition to these water quality state variables, the model also solves for pH and the carbonate cycle (CO₂, HCO₃, H₂CO₃) as part of the set of derived water quality variables.

The source/sink term [CSSK] represents a mass rate of change (model code internal units of g m⁻³ s⁻¹) of a constituent due to kinetic reactions where concentrations are expressed as g m⁻³ or mg/L. All rate inputs from the control file are in units of day⁻¹ and are then converted to s⁻¹ before being used in the code. The sources/sinks for constituents are separated into two arrays, [CSSB] and [CSSK]. [CSSB] contains boundary sources/sinks. [CSSK] contains internal sources/sinks due to kinetic interactions. The frequency at which kinetic sources/sinks [CSSK] are updated is specified by the parameter [CUF].

The model can simulate any combination of the following constituent groups:

  • Generic constituents (conservative tracers, volatile substances)
  • Bacteria
  • Dissolved gases (N₂, total dissolved gas)
  • Water age or residence time
  • CH₄, H₂S, SO₄
  • Fe²⁺, FeOOH, Mn²⁺, MnO₂
  • Inorganic suspended solids (ISS)
  • Total dissolved solids (TDS) or salinity
  • Dissolved organic matter (labile DOM, refractory DOM)
  • Particulate organic matter (labile POM, refractory POM)
  • Organic matter variable stoichiometry (LDOM-P, RDOM-P, LPOM-P, RPOM-P, LDOM-N, RDOM-N, LPOM-N, RPOM-N)
  • Organic carbon constituents (LPOC, RPOC, LDOC, RDOC)
  • Carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD, CBODP, CBODN)
  • Algae (multiple groups with vertical migration and toxin production)
  • Periphyton/Epiphyton
  • Macrophytes
  • Zooplankton
  • Phosphorus (PO₄)
  • Ammonium (NH₄)
  • Nitrate-Nitrite (NO₃ + NO₂)
  • Dissolved silica, Particulate biogenic silica
  • Dissolved oxygen (including reaeration)
  • Organic sediments (zero-order and first-order models)
  • Sediment variable stoichiometry (P, N, C)
  • Sediment diagenesis model
  • Total inorganic carbon, alkalinity, pH, and carbonate species
  • Temperature rate multipliers

docs.title: Generic Constituent
docs.text:
Any number of generic constituents [NGC] can be defined (Figure 63) that can settle, decay (using either zero order and/or first order decay and/or photochemical reactions), transfer across the air/water interface, and/or be released from the sediment during anoxic conditions (just for the zero order SOD model). Generic constituents do not interact with the hydrodynamics nor any other water quality state variables.

Figure 63. Internal flux for generic constituent compartment.

The source/sink term for a generic constituent is:

\[ S_g = -K_0\theta^{(T-20)} - K_1\theta^{(T-20)}\Phi_g - \omega_g\frac{\partial \Phi_g}{\partial z} - \alpha I_o(1-\beta)e^{-\lambda z}\Phi_g + \frac{A_{sur}}{V_{sur}}K_L(\Phi_s - \Phi_g) + K_{sedrel}SOD\frac{A}{V} \tag{4-64} \]

where:

  • \(\theta\) = temperature rate multiplier
  • \(T\) = water temperature, °C
  • \(\alpha\) = photodegradation parameter, m²/J
  • \(I_o\) = radiation at surface, W m⁻²
  • \(\lambda\) = light extinction coefficient, m⁻¹
  • \(\beta\) = fraction of short-wave solar absorbed on the surface
  • \(\omega_g\) = settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_0\) = zero order decay coefficient, g m⁻³ s⁻¹ at 20 °C
  • \(K_1\) = first order decay coefficient, s⁻¹ at 20 °C
  • \(\Phi_g\) = generic constituent concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_s\) = generic constituent concentration gas saturation in the atmosphere, g m⁻³
  • \(A_{sur}\) = surface area, m²
  • \(V_{sur}\) = surface volume, m³
  • \(A\) = cell bottom surface area, m²
  • \(V\) = cell volume, m³
  • \(K_L\) = surface gas transfer coefficient, m/s
  • \(K_{sedrel}\) = sediment release as a fraction of SOD (zero order model), (-)
  • \(SOD\) = temperature corrected sediment oxygen demand (zero order model), m/s

Photodegradation can be an important mechanism for constituents such as fecal coliforms (Mitchell and Chamberlain, 1978; Auer and Niehaus, 1993) and dissolved organic matter (Moran and Zepp, 1996; Reche et al., 1999). The photo decay rate can be modeled as a pseudo 1st order decay (k_light) rate, as described by:

\[ \frac{\delta C}{\delta t} = -k_{light} \times C \]

where k_light is the first-order decay coefficient (s⁻¹) and C is the constituent concentration (g/m³). Chamberlin and Mitchell (1978) defined the light-induced decay of coliforms based on Beer's Law and a proportionality constant as:

\[ k_{light} = \alpha \, I_0 \, e^{-\lambda z} \]

where α is the user-defined proportionality constant for the effect of incident light on a specific constituent or organism, I₀ is the incident light energy at the water surface (cal/cm²-day), λ is the light attenuation coefficient per unit depth (m⁻¹), and z is the depth below the water surface (m). Table 10 shows a selection of α values reported in the literature for coliforms (Bowie et al., 1985). The CE-QUAL-W2 model uses units of W/m² for radiation; hence the corresponding units of alpha as used in the CE-QUAL-W2 model are m²/J.

Table 10. Comparison of α estimates based on Chamberlin and Mitchell (1978) with additional values (Bowie et al., 1985).

Organism Study α (cm²/cal) α (m²/J) Data Source Coliform Group 14 field studies (mean) 0.481 1.15E-05 Gameson and Gould (1975) Coliform Group 24 field studies (mean) 0.168 4.01E-06 Foxworthy and Kneeling (1969) Coliform Group 61 laboratory studies (mean) 0.136 3.25E-06 Gameson and Gould (1975) Fecal Coliform Estimated from field and laboratory studies (mean of salt and freshwater) 0.042 1.00E-06 Mancini (1978) Fecal Coliforms 22 chamber studies in freshwater (mean) 0.005 1.19E-07 Lantrip (1983) Total Coliforms 22 chamber studies in freshwater (mean) 0.004 9.55E-08 Lantrip (1983)

A conservative tracer, coliform bacteria, N₂ gas (and Total Dissolved Gas), a volatile generic constituent, and water age are some of the state variables that can be modeled using the generic constituent and are described further below.

docs.title: Conservative Tracer
docs.text:
A conservative constituent is included to allow dye study simulations, movements of conservative materials through the waterbody, and as an aid in calibrating and testing flow regimes. This constituent has no internal sources or sinks and the rate term [CSSK] is set to zero.

\[ S_{tracer} = 0 \tag{4-65} \]

docs.title: Volatile Generic Constituent
docs.text:
The loss of a volatile generic constituent, such as a hydrocarbon, by volatilization from the water surface is simulated using the same algorithms as used for N₂. The rate at which a generic constituent molecule enters and leaves the water surface is described by:

\[ S_{vol} = \frac{A_{sur}}{Vol_{cell}}K_{Lg}(\phi_{sg} - \phi_g) = \frac{1}{h_{KT}}K_{Lg}(\phi_{sg} - \phi_g) \]

where:

  • \(K_{Lg}\) = surface gas transfer coefficient for a generic constituent, m/s
  • \(A_{sur}\) = surface area of the surface layer computational cell, m²
  • \(Vol_{cell}\) = volume of the surface layer computational cell, m³
  • \(h_{KT}\) = depth of the surface layer (K=KT) computational cell, m
  • \(\phi_g\) = liquid phase generic constituent concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\phi_{sg}\) = hypothetical saturation liquid phase generic constituent concentration if in equilibrium with the gas phase, g m⁻³

The gas transfer rate coefficient can be estimated based on the reaeration rate for oxygen:

\[ K_{Lg} = K_{LO2}\sqrt{\frac{D_g}{D_{O2}}} \]

The molecular diffusion coefficients can be related to their molecular weights: \(\frac{D_g}{D_{O2}} = \sqrt{\frac{MW_{O2}}{MW_g}}\). Hence: \(K_{Lg} = K_{LO2}\left(\frac{MW_{O2}}{MW_g}\right)^{0.25} = K_{LO2} \times CGKLF\) where CGKLF is the user-defined gas transfer factor.

Table 11. CGKLF input values for hydrocarbons, CO₂, and N₂.

Chemical MW (g/mole) CGKLF Nitrogen 28.01 1.034 Carbon Dioxide 44 0.923 Benzene 78.11 0.800 MTBE 88.15 0.776 Toluene 92.13 0.768 Ethylbenzene 106.16 0.741

docs.title: Bacteria
docs.text:
Coliform bacteria are commonly used as an indicator of pathogen contamination (Figure 64). Safety standards and criteria for drinking and recreational purposes are based upon coliform concentrations.

Figure 64. Internal flux for coliform bacteria.

Total coliform, fecal coliform, fecal streptococci, and/or any other type of bacteria that do not interact with other state variables can be simulated. The rate equation for bacteria is (including photodegradation):

\[ S_g = -K_{col}\theta^{(T-20)}\Phi_{col} - \omega_{col}\frac{\partial \Phi_{col}}{\partial z} - \alpha I_o(1-\beta)e^{-\lambda z}\Phi_{col} \]

where:

  • \(\theta\) = temperature factor (Q10)
  • \(T\) = water temperature, °C
  • \(K_{col}\) = coliform mortality rate, s⁻¹ at 20 °C
  • \(\Phi_{col}\) = coliform concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\omega_{col}\) = bacteria settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(\alpha\) = photodegradation parameter, m²/J
  • \(I_o\) = radiation at surface, W m⁻²
  • \(\lambda\) = light extinction coefficient, m⁻¹
  • \(\beta\) = fraction of short-wave solar absorbed on the surface
  • \(z\) = water depth, m

docs.title: Dissolved Nitrogen Gas and Total Dissolved Gas
N₂ Dissolved Gas
docs.text:
N₂ gas is a state variable and is modeled by internally computing the N₂ gas saturation as a function of temperature and air humidity and internally computing the gas transfer coefficient (for reaeration). The sink term is just gas transfer as shown in Figure 65:

\[ S_{N2} = \frac{A_{sur}}{V_{sur}}K_{LN2}(\Phi_{sN2} - \Phi_{N2}) \tag{4-67} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{N2}\) = N₂ generic constituent concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{sN2}\) = N₂ gas saturation concentration in the atmosphere, g m⁻³
  • \(A_{sur}\) = surface area, m²
  • \(V_{sur}\) = surface volume, m³
  • \(K_{LN2}\) = surface gas transfer coefficient for N₂, m/s
Figure 65. N₂ gas exchange.

Nitrogen gas is a slightly soluble gas, like oxygen. Using the Higbie-Penetration theory (Chapra, 1997), \(K_{LN2} = K_{LO2}\sqrt{\frac{D_{N2}}{D_{O2}}}\) and since \(\frac{D_{N2}}{D_{O2}} = \sqrt{\frac{MW_{O2}}{MW_{N2}}}\), then \(K_{LN2} = K_{LO2}\left(\frac{MW_{O2}}{MW_{N2}}\right)^{0.25} = 1.034K_{LO2}\) where MWO2 = 32 g/mole and MWN2 = 28 g/mole.

The value of N₂ saturation, \(\Phi_{sN2}\), is determined using Henry's Law: \(x_{N2} = K_H P_{N2}\) where \(x_{N2}\) is the mole fraction of nitrogen gas, \(K_H\) is Henry's Law constant in moles/atm, and \(P_{N2}\) is the partial pressure of N₂ gas in the atmosphere in atm. Nitrogen gas is assumed to be 79% of the total gas composition in the atmosphere for dry air. Atmospheric pressure changes with altitude are accounted for using:

\[ P(atm) = \left[1 - \frac{Altitude, km}{44.3}\right]^{5.25} \]

Combining with Henry's Law: \(C_{N2} = 55.6 \times 28 \times 10^3 P_{N2} K_H = 1.5568E6 \cdot P_{N2} K_H\). The Henry's Law constant is temperature dependent (Figure 66): \(K_H(\text{atm}^{-1}) = 1.8816E\text{-}005 - 4.116E\text{-}007 \times T + 4.6E\text{-}009 \times T^2\) where T is the surface temperature in °C.

Figure 66. Henry's Law constant dependence on temperature.

The %N₂ in the atmosphere needs to be corrected for water vapor. The vapor pressure (Figure 67) is computed using the air temperature in °C as (Chapra, 1997): \(P_{watervapor}(mmHg) = 4.596\exp\left(\frac{17.27T}{237.3+T}\right)\). Figure 68 shows the atmospheric pressure correction. The relative humidity (RH) was computed based on dew point temperature, \(T_d\), and air temperature, T: (Singh, 1992): \(RH = \left[\frac{112 - 0.1T + T_d}{112 + 0.9T}\right]^8\).

Figure 67. Vapor pressure as a function of air temperature and relative humidity. Figure 68. Atmospheric pressure correction as a result of vapor pressure correction assuming original atmospheric pressure is 1 atm.

docs.title: Total Dissolved Gas
docs.text:
Once N₂ gas is used in the model, the derived constituent TDG% can also be turned ON. TDG, % is computed from:

\[ TDG, \% = \left(\frac{0.79 \times N2\ concentration}{N2\ saturation\ concentration} + \frac{0.21 \times O2\ concentration}{O2\ saturation\ concentration}\right)100 \]

N₂ gas can be entrained at hydropower facilities and at dams. Algorithms for adding dissolved gas at these facilities is outlined under Dissolved Oxygen/Dam Reaeration.

docs.title: Water Age or Residence Time
docs.text:
The water age is used to compute how long water has remained in the modeled domain. This is accomplished by using only a zero-order decay rate set to -1 day⁻¹. This results in a state variable that increases by 1 day⁻¹, which is an exact representation of water age or hydraulic residence time (Figure 69).

\[ S_{age} = -1\ day^{-1} \tag{4-68} \] Figure 69. Water age in Chester Morse Lake, WA.

docs.title: Dissolved Gas Pressure
docs.text:
The model computes dissolved gas pressure (DGP in atm) which is used to compute Total Dissolved Gas (TDG) from TDG = 100*DGP/PALT where PALT is the atmospheric pressure in atm at the water surface. This state variable can be used in lieu of using dissolved oxygen and dissolved nitrogen gas as state variables if the model user is only interested in modeling production of dissolved gas at spillways and the gas transfer downstream.

The DGP exchange at the air-water interface is modeled as a first order rate process:

\[ \frac{dDGP}{dt} = -k_{DGP}(DGP - P_{atm}) \]

where DGP is dissolved gas pressure (atm), \(P_{atm}\) is barometric pressure (atm), and \(k_{DGP}\) is the air/water gas exchange rate (d⁻¹). For lakes or estuaries: \(k_{DGP} = DGPO2\frac{K_L}{H}\) where \(K_L\) is the reaeration coefficient (m/d), H is the depth of the surface layer (m), and DGPO2 is the ratio of dissolved gas to oxygen surface transfer ratio. A typical value of DGPO2 would be 1.027 assuming 0.21 O₂ and 0.79 N₂ gas composition.

The TDG saturation can also be calculated from normalizing the DGP by the local barometric pressure: \(TDG\% = 100\frac{DGP}{P_{atm}}\).

docs.title: Water Column CH₄, H₂S, SO₄
docs.text:
Methane (CH₄) and hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) constituents are state variables for the water column. CH₄ is modeled as mg/L as C. H₂S is modeled as mg/L as S. For both constituents, the anaerobic release from the sediments, aerobic decay, and reaeration were modeled (Figure 70 and Figure 71).

Figure 70. Sources and sinks for methane. Figure 71. Sources and sinks for hydrogen sulfide and sulfate.

The rate equations for methane and hydrogen sulfide were identical, except for different parameter values and assuming saturation values in the atmosphere of 0 mg/L for both gases:

\[ S = SOD\gamma_{OM}\delta_{SODR}\frac{A_{sed}}{V} + A_{sur}K_L(-\Phi) - \theta^{T-20}K\Phi_C \]

where:

  • \(A_{sed}\) = sediment surface area, m²
  • \(A_{sur}\) = surface area of surface computational cell, m²
  • \(SOD\) = zero-order sediment oxygen demand, g m⁻² s⁻¹
  • \(K_L\) = interfacial exchange rate, m s⁻¹
  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = organic matter temperature rate multiplier
  • \(\delta_{SODR}\) = sediment release rate of H₂S or CH₄, fraction of zero-order SOD
  • \(\Phi\) = constituent concentration (H₂S or CH₄), g m⁻³
  • \(\theta\) = temperature rate multiplier
  • \(T\) = temperature, °C
  • \(K\) = decay rate, s⁻¹

The oxidation of CH₄ was based on the stoichiometric relationship: CH₄ + 2O₂ → 2H₂O + CO₂

The oxidation of H₂S in the water column was based on: H₂S + 2O₂ → SO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺

The reaeration coefficient for H₂S is: \(k_{H2S} = k_{O2}\left(\frac{MW_{O2}}{MW_{H2S}}\right)^{0.25} = k_{O2} \times 0.984\) (MWH2S = 34.08 g/mol). The reaeration coefficient for CH₄ is: \(k_{CH4} = k_{O2}\left(\frac{MW_{O2}}{MW_{CH4}}\right)^{0.25} = k_{O2} \times 1.188\) (MWCH4 = 16.04 g/mol).

When the sediment diagenesis model is active, the release rates of CH₄ and H₂S are computed directly from this model rather than using the zero-order SOD model.

docs.title: Water Column Fe²⁺, FeOOH, Mn²⁺, MnO₂
docs.text:
The state variables of Fe and Mn in the water column are Fe(II), FeOOH, Mn(II), and MnO₂. These interact with the sediments in the sediment diagenesis model. In the water column the processes active are shown in Figure 72 for Fe and Figure 73 for Mn.

Figure 72. Sources and sinks of Fe in the water column. Figure 73. Sources and sinks of Mn in the water column.

docs.title: Ferrous Iron Fe²⁺
docs.text:
The rate equation in the water column for Fe(II) is:

\[ S_{Fe(II)} = -\underbrace{k_{Fe(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Fe(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} + \underbrace{k_{FeOOH}\left(\frac{K_{FeOOH}}{K_{FeOOH} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{FeOOH}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

where:

  • \(k_{FeOOH}\) = reduction rate in water column, s⁻¹
  • \(k_{Fe(II)0}\) = oxidation rate in water column, s⁻¹ (g m⁻³)⁻¹
  • \(K_{FeOOH}\) = half-saturation constant for oxygen for this reaction, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{DO}\) = dissolved oxygen concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{Fe(II)}\) = ferrous iron concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{FeOOH}\) = iron oxyhydroxide concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(pH\) = pH in water column

docs.title: Iron Oxyhydroxide FeOOH
docs.text:
The rate equation in the water column for iron oxyhydroxide is:

\[ S_{FeOOH} = \underbrace{k_{Fe(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Fe(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} - \underbrace{k_{FeOOH}\left(\frac{K_{FeOOH}}{K_{FeOOH} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{FeOOH}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

docs.title: Mn²⁺ (Divalent Manganese)
docs.text:
The rate equation for Mn(II) in the water column is:

\[ S_{Mn(II)} = -\underbrace{k_{Mn(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Mn(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} + \underbrace{k_{MnO_2}\left(\frac{K_{MnO_2}}{K_{MnO_2} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{MnO_2}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

where:

  • \(k_{MnO_2}\) = reduction rate in water column, s⁻¹
  • \(k_{Mn(II)0}\) = oxidation rate in water column, s⁻¹ (g m⁻³)⁻¹
  • \(K_{MnO_2}\) = half-saturation constant for oxygen for this reaction, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{Mn(II)}\) = Mn(II) concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{MnO_2}\) = manganese dioxide concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Manganese Dioxide MnO₂
docs.text:
The rate equation in the water column for manganese dioxide is:

\[ S_{MnO_2} = \underbrace{k_{Mn(II)0}\Phi_{DO} 10^{2(pH-7)} \Phi_{Mn(II)}}_{\text{Oxidation}} - \underbrace{k_{MnO_2}\left(\frac{K_{MnO_2}}{K_{MnO_2} + \Phi_{DO}}\right)\Phi_{MnO_2}}_{\text{Reduction}} \]

docs.title: Inorganic Suspended Solids
docs.text:
Inorganic suspended solids [ISS] are important in water quality simulations because of their influence on density, light penetration, and nutrient availability. Increased solids concentrations reduce light penetration in the water column thus affecting temperature that in turn affects biological and chemical reaction rates. Dissolved phosphorus and silica concentrations can also be affected by solids through sorption and settling. Light and nutrient availability largely control algal production.

The settling velocity of each inorganic suspended solids compartment is a user-defined parameter (Figure 74). Usually this is determined from Stokes' settling velocity for a particular sediment diameter and specific gravity. Any number of inorganic suspended solids groups can be modeled.

Figure 74. Internal flux for inorganic suspended solids.

The rate equation for inorganic suspended solids is:

\[ S_{ISS} = \omega_{ISS}\frac{\partial \Phi_{ISS}}{\partial z} \tag{4-69} \]

where:

  • \(z\) = layer thickness, m
  • \(\omega_{ISS}\) = settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{ISS}\) = inorganic suspended solids concentration, g m⁻³

In the finite difference representation of suspended solids concentrations, solids settling from layer [K]-1 serve as a source for the layer below it [K]. Typical settling rates can be computed using Stokes' Law. Figure 75 shows typical settling rates based on particle diameter and density.

Figure 75. Typical settling of particles based on Stokes' Law based on particle diameter and density.

Multiple ISS groups can be defined with different settling velocities and particle sizes. When ISS settles to the bottom, it is lost from the water column. Unlike organic sediments, ISS does not accumulate in the sediment compartment.

Note

In the sediment diagenesis model for Version 4.22 and earlier, there was a group for Mature Fine Tailings that was added as a generic constituent. The current model now sets this state variable as a suspended solids group.

docs.title: Total Dissolved Solids or Salinity
docs.text:
Total dissolved solids (TDS) affect water density and ionic strength, thereby affecting water movements, pH, and the distribution of carbonate species. Dissolved solids are normally expressed as TDS in freshwater applications. Estuarine applications normally use salinity.

Either TDS or salinity can be used with the choice indicated by the parameter [WTYPEC] specified in the control file. If TDS is used, the units are g m⁻³; if salinity is used, the units are kg m⁻³. TDS and salinity are not necessarily equivalent. In the model, both are treated conservatively with the rate term set to zero.

docs.title: Labile DOM
docs.text:
Because of the importance of dissolved oxygen in aquatic systems, all constituents exerting an oxygen demand must be included in kinetic formulations. This demand is often measured as the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which includes microbial respiration and metabolism of various organic and inorganic compounds. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is composed of labile and refractory components (Figure 76). DOM is modeled as two separate compartments because of the different decomposition rates of the two groups.

Figure 76. Internal flux between labile DOM and other compartments.

The rate equation for labile DOM is:

\[ S_{LDOM} = \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{am})K_{am}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{em})K_{em}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{LDOM}\Phi_{LDOM}}_{\text{labile DOM decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{mm})K_{mm}\Phi_{macro}}_{\text{macrophyte mortality/excretion}} \tag{4-70} \]

where:

  • \(P_{am}\) = pattern coefficient for algal mortality
  • \(P_{em}\) = pattern coefficient for epiphyton mortality
  • \(P_{mm}\) = partitioning coefficient for macrophyte mortality
  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier for organic matter decay
  • \(K_{ae}\) = algal excretion rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{am}\) = algal mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{ee}\) = epiphyton excretion rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{em}\) = epiphyton mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{mm}\) = macrophyte mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LDOM}\) = labile DOM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = labile to refractory DOM transfer rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_a\) = algal concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_e\) = epiphyton concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{LDOM}\) = labile DOM concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{macro}\) = macrophyte concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Refractory DOM
docs.text:
Refractory DOM is composed of compounds in the aquatic environment that slowly decompose, exerting oxygen demand over long periods (Figure 77). Internally, refractory DOM is produced from the decomposition of labile DOM.

Figure 77. Internal flux between refractory DOM and other compartments.

The rate equation for refractory DOM is:

\[ S_{RDOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RDOM}\Phi_{RDOM}}_{\text{decay}} \tag{4-71} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier
  • \(K_{RDOM}\) = refractory DOM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = transfer rate from labile DOM, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{LDOM}\) = labile DOM concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{RDOM}\) = refractory DOM concentration, g m⁻³

The rate terms are evaluated in subroutine REFRACTORY_DOM.

docs.title: Labile POM
docs.text:
Labile particulate organic matter (LPOM) represents particulate organic material in the water column. Decaying particulate organic matter is a source of refractory particulate organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus, and inorganic carbon. A stoichiometric relationship governs mineralization of ammonium, phosphorus, and inorganic carbon, and an oxygen demand is exerted as LPOM decomposes.

When LPOM settles to the bottom, it accumulates and decays in the sediment compartment or the sediment diagenesis compartment if activated for the simulation (Figure 78).

Figure 78. Internal flux between labile POM and other compartments.

The rate equation for LPOM is:

\[ S_{LPOM} = \underbrace{\sum P_{am}K_{am}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{em}K_{em}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} - \underbrace{K_{LPOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LPOM}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial A\Phi_{LPOM}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}K_{mm}\Phi_{macro}}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zm}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}(1-Z_{effic})\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton excretion}} - \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}\left(\frac{\sigma_{pom}}{\sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo} + \sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}\right)\Phi_{LPOM}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton ingestion of LPOM}} \tag{4-72} \]

where:

  • \(P_{am}\) = partition coefficient for algal mortality
  • \(P_{em}\) = partition coefficient for epiphyton mortality
  • \(P_{mm}\) = partition coefficient for macrophyte mortality
  • \(P_{zooP}\) = partition coefficient for zooplankton LPOM grazing
  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier for organic matter
  • \(\omega_{POM}\) = POM settling rate, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_{am}\) = algal mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{em}\) = epiphyton mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{mm}\) = macrophyte mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{zm}\) = zooplankton mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{zg}\) = zooplankton growth rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LPOM}\) = labile POM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{effic}\) = zooplankton ingestion efficiency
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = transfer rate from labile POM to refractory POM, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_a\) = algal concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_e\) = periphyton/epiphyton concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{macro}\) = macrophyte concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{LPOM}\) = detritus concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{zoo}\) = zooplankton concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\sigma_{pom}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for particulate organic matter
  • \(\sigma_{alg}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for algae
  • \(\sigma_{zoo}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for zooplankton

POM settling and accumulation in the sediment compartment is handled identically to the algal compartment.

docs.title: Refractory POM
docs.text:
Refractory POM is slowly decaying non-living, organic matter that settles (Figure 79). The source/sink terms are first-order decay, the conversion of LPOM to RPOM, and sedimentation. The settled organic matter becomes part of the first-order sediment model or the sediment diagenesis model if they are active.

Figure 79. Internal flux between refractory POM and other compartments.

The rate equation for RPOM is:

\[ S_{RPOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RPOM}\Phi_{RPOM}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{RPOM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOM}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-73} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{OM}\) = temperature rate multiplier
  • \(K_{L \to R}\) = transfer rate from labile POM to refractory POM, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{RPOM}\) = refractory POM decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\omega_{POM}\) = POM settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{LPOM}\) = labile POM concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{RPOM}\) = refractory POM concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Organic Matter Variable Stoichiometry
docs.text:
CE-QUAL-W2 includes variable stoichiometry of organic matter starting with Version 3.5. Previous versions used fixed stoichiometric constants for the ratios of nitrogen and phosphorus to organic matter.

Eight constituents are required to simulate the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus in labile dissolved organic matter (LDOM), refractory organic matter (RDOM), labile particulate organic matter (LPOM), and refractory particulate organic matter (RPOM). These constituents are summarized in the following table. All inputs of organic matter accumulate N and P according to the stoichiometry of the incoming organic matter.

Abbreviation Constituent LDOM-P Labile dissolved organic matter phosphorus RDOM-P Refractory dissolved organic matter phosphorus LPOM-P Labile particulate organic matter phosphorus RPOM-P Refractory particulate organic matter phosphorus LDOM-N Labile dissolved organic matter nitrogen RDOM-N Refractory dissolved organic matter nitrogen LPOM-N Labile particulate organic matter nitrogen RPOM-N Refractory particulate organic matter nitrogen

docs.title: LDOM-P
docs.text:
LDOM-P is the amount of phosphorus in labile dissolved organic matter. The rate equation for LDOM-P is:

\[ S_{\text{LDOM-P}} = \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\delta_{Pa}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{am})K_{am}\delta_{Pa}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\delta_{Pe}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{em})K_{em}\delta_{Pe}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{mm})K_{mm}\delta_{Pm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{K_{LDOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-P}}_{\text{labile DOM-P decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM-P decay}}} \tag{4-74} \]

docs.title: RDOM-P
docs.text:
The rate equation for RDOM-P is:

\[ S_{RDOM-P} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RDOM}\Phi_{RDOM-P}}_{\text{decay}} \tag{4-75} \]

docs.title: LPOM-P
docs.text:
The rate equation for LPOM-P is:

\[ S_{LPOM-P} = \underbrace{\sum P_{am}K_{am}\delta_{Pa}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{em}K_{em}\delta_{Pe}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}P_{mpom}K_{mm}\delta_{Pm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zm}\delta_{Pz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{K_{LPOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LPOM-P}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}(1-Z_{effic})\delta_{Pz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton excretion}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}\frac{\Phi_{LPOM-P}}{\Phi_{LPOM}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}{\sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo} + \sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}\right)\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton ingestion}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{LPOM-P}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-76} \]

docs.title: RPOM-P
docs.text:
The rate equation for RPOM-P is:

\[ S_{RPOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-P}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RPOM}\Phi_{RPOM-P}}_{\text{decay}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}(1-P_{mpom})K_{mm}\delta_{Pm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOM-P}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-77} \]

docs.title: LDOM-N
docs.text:
LDOM-N is the amount of nitrogen in labile dissolved organic matter. The rate equation for LDOM-N is:

\[ S_{\text{LDOM-N}} = \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\delta_{Na}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{am})K_{am}\delta_{Na}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\delta_{Ne}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{em})K_{em}\delta_{Ne}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum(1-P_{mm})K_{mm}\delta_{Nm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{K_{LDOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-N}}_{\text{labile DOM-N decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LDOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM-N decay}}} \tag{4-78} \]

docs.title: RDOM-N
docs.text:
The rate equation for RDOM-N is:

\[ S_{RDOM-N} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LDOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RDOM}\Phi_{RDOM-N}}_{\text{decay}} \tag{4-79} \]

docs.title: LPOM-N
docs.text:
The rate equation for LPOM-N is:

\[ S_{LPOM-N} = \underbrace{\sum P_{am}K_{am}\delta_{Na}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{em}K_{em}\delta_{Ne}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}P_{mpom}K_{mm}\delta_{Nm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{K_{zm}\delta_{Nz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{K_{LPOM}\gamma_{OM}\Phi_{LPOM-N}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}(1-Z_{effic})\delta_{Nz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton excretion}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\sum K_{zg}\frac{\Phi_{LPOM-N}}{\Phi_{LPOM}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}{\sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo} + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{LPOM}}\right)\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton ingestion}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{LPOM-N}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-80} \]

docs.title: RPOM-N
docs.text:
The rate equation for RPOM-N is:

\[ S_{RPOM} = \underbrace{K_{L \to R}\Phi_{LPOM-N}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POM decay}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{RPOM}\Phi_{RPOM-N}}_{\text{decay}} + \underbrace{\sum P_{mm}(1-P_{mpom})K_{mm}\delta_{Nm}\Phi_m}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} - \underbrace{\omega_{POM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOM-N}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-81} \]

docs.title: Organic Carbon Constituents
docs.text:
The organic matter state variables (LPOM, RPOM, RDOM, LDOM) are based on organic matter dry weight. CE-QUAL-W2 also supports organic matter expressed as carbon (C). Many other models use this approach because organic matter is rarely measured in the field, whereas organic carbon is routinely measured. Instead of LDOM, LPOM, RDOM, and RPOM, the user can specify LDOC, LPOC, RDOC, and RPOC.

Organic matter is difficult for laboratories to measure directly (Figure 80). However, collective water quality parameters such as organic carbon, organic nitrogen, and organic phosphorus are commonly measured. The model includes an option for directly simulating organic carbon constituents without organic matter. The four organic carbon state variables are labile dissolved organic carbon (LDOC), refractory dissolved organic carbon (RDOC), labile particulate organic carbon (LPOC), and refractory particulate organic carbon (RPOC).

docs.title: LPOC
docs.text:
Figure 80. Kinetics of LPOC in the water column.

The kinetic source/sink term for LPOC is:

\[ S_{LPOC} = \underbrace{\sum K_{am}\delta_{ca}\Phi_a P_{am}}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{em}\delta_{ce}\Phi_e P_{em}}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} - \underbrace{\omega_{LPOM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{LPOC}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOC}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\text{LPOC decay}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POC transfer}}} + \underbrace{\gamma_{OM}K_{LPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\text{LPOC hydrolysis}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{mm}\delta_{cm}\Phi_{macro}P_{nom}P_{mmLPOM}}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{K_{zm}\delta_{cz}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{zooplankton mortality}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\sum\left(Z_u\delta_{cz}\Phi_{zoo}\frac{\Phi_{LPOM}}{\sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \Phi_{LPOM} + \sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo}}\right)}_{\text{zooplankton growth}} \tag{4-82} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{LPOC}\) = LPOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(P_{am}\) = fraction of algal mortality into LPOM (0--1)
  • \(P_{em}\) = fraction of epiphyton mortality into LPOM (0--1)
  • \(P_{mm}\) = fraction of macrophyte mortality into LPOM (0--1)
  • \(\delta_{ca}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in algae, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(\delta_{ce}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in epiphyton, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(\delta_{cm}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in macrophyte, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(\delta_{cz}\) = stoichiometric ratio of carbon in zooplankton, g C (g DW)⁻¹
  • \(K_{LPOC}\) = LPOC decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\) = transfer rate from LPOC to RPOC, s⁻¹

docs.title: RPOC
docs.text:
The kinetics of RPOC in the water column are shown in Figure 81.

Figure 81. Kinetics of RPOC in the water column.

The kinetic source/sink term for RPOC is:

\[ S_{RPOC} = \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{POC transfer}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RPOC}\Phi_{RPOC}}_{\text{RPOC decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{RPOM}\frac{\partial \Phi_{RPOC}}{\partial z}}_{\text{RPOC settling}} \] \[ - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{RPOC}}_{\text{RPOC hydrolysis}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{mm}\delta_{cm}\Phi_{macro}P_{mm}(1-P_{mmLPOM})}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} \tag{4-83} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{RPOC}\) = RPOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(K_{LPOC \to RPOC}\) = transfer rate from LPOC to RPOC, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{RPOC}\) = RPOC decay rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: LDOC
docs.text:
The kinetics of LDOC in the water column are shown in Figure 82.

Figure 82. Kinetics of LDOC in the water column.

The kinetic source/sink term for LDOC is:

\[ S_{LDOC} = \underbrace{\sum K_{am}\delta_{ca}\Phi_a(1-P_{am})}_{\text{algal mortality}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{ae}\delta_{ca}\Phi_a}_{\text{algal excretion}} + \underbrace{\sum K_{em}\delta_{ce}\Phi_e(1-P_{em})}_{\text{epiphyton mortality}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum K_{ee}\delta_{ce}\Phi_e}_{\text{epiphyton excretion}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LDOC}\Phi_{LDOC}}_{\text{LDOC decay}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\Phi_{LDOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOC transfer}}} \] \[ + \underbrace{\sum K_{mm}\delta_{cm}\Phi_{macro}(1-P_{mm})}_{\text{macrophyte mortality}} + \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{LPOC}}_{\text{LPOC hydrolysis}} + \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RPOM \to LDOM}\Phi_{RPOC}}_{\text{RPOC hydrolysis}} \tag{4-84} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{LDOC}\) = LDOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(K_{LDOC}\) = LDOC decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\) = LDOC to RDOC transfer rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: RDOC
docs.text:
The kinetics of RDOC in the water column are shown in Figure 83.

Figure 83. Kinetics of RDOC in the water column.

The kinetic source/sink term for RDOC is:

\[ S_{RDOC} = \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\Phi_{LDOC}}_{\substack{\text{labile to refractory} \\ \text{DOC transfer}}} - \underbrace{\gamma_{om}K_{RDOC}\Phi_{RDOC}}_{\text{RDOC decay}} \tag{4-85} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{RDOC}\) = RDOC concentration, g C m⁻³
  • \(K_{RDOC}\) = RDOC decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{LDOC \to RDOC}\) = LDOC to RDOC transfer rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: Carbonaceous Biochemical Oxygen Demand (CBOD)
docs.text:
Any number of CBOD groups with varying decay rates and either particulate or dissolved can be modeled, allowing the user to more accurately characterize various CBOD sources. Additionally, different CBOD sources can be tracked separately in the model to determine their effect on the receiving water.

When including CBOD in the simulation, ensure that CBOD, DOM, POM, and algal biomass are properly accounted for to avoid double-counting oxygen demand. CBOD is typically specified as allochthonous inputs, while autochthonous organic matter is tracked in the various organic matter compartments. This group can model dissolved or particulate CBOD by specifying a zero or a finite settling velocity, respectively. Settled CBOD enters the first-order sediment compartment.

In Version 3.6 and earlier (Figure 85), the CBOD cycle used fixed stoichiometry in terms of C:N:P. Starting with Version 3.7, the nitrogen and phosphorus corresponding to each CBOD group are modeled as separate constituents.

Figure 85. Internal flux between CBOD and other compartments in Version 3.7 and later.

The rate equation for CBOD is:

\[ S_{CBOD} = -\underbrace{\Theta^{T-20}K_{BOD}R_{BOD}\Phi_{CBOD}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{CBOD}\frac{\partial R_{BOD}\Phi_{CBOD}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \tag{4-86} \]

where:

  • \(\Theta\) = BOD temperature rate multiplier
  • \(T\) = temperature, °C
  • \(\omega_{CBOD}\) = CBOD settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_{BOD}\) = CBOD decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(R_{BOD}\) = CBOD conversion from input CBOD to CBOD-ultimate (CBODᵤ)
  • \(\Phi_{CBOD}\) = CBOD concentration, g m⁻³

Note

The model accepts 5-day CBOD₅ or any other day CBOD as input. The \(R_{BOD}\) term converts to CBODᵤ (ultimate or 28-day) internally. The model outputs CBOD in the same form as the input (e.g., CBOD₅ if CBOD₅ was entered). If CBODᵤ is used as input, set \(R_{BOD}\) = 1.

Typical determination of \(R_{BOD}\) is based on the following standard CBOD equation:

\[ R_{BOD} = \frac{CBOD_u}{CBOD_t} = \frac{1}{1 - \exp(-K_{BOD} t)} \]

where \(t\) is the time in days (5 days, for example), \(K_{BOD}\) is the BOD decay rate in day⁻¹, and \(CBOD_t\) is the CBOD at that time.

docs.title: CBODP
docs.text:
The phosphorus associated with a specific CBOD group is modeled as a separate constituent. The rate equation for CBODP is:

\[ S_{CBODP} = -\underbrace{\Theta^{T-20}K_{BOD}\Phi_{CBODP}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{CBOD}\frac{\partial \Phi_{CBODP}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \]

where:

  • \(\Theta\) = BOD temperature rate multiplier
  • \(T\) = temperature, °C
  • \(\omega_{CBOD}\) = CBOD settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_{BOD}\) = CBOD decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{CBODP}\) = CBODP concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: CBODN
docs.text:
The nitrogen associated with a specific CBOD group is modeled as a separate constituent. The rate equation for CBODN is:

\[ S_{CBODN} = -\underbrace{\Theta^{T-20}K_{BOD}\Phi_{CBODN}}_{\text{decay}} - \underbrace{\omega_{CBOD}\frac{\partial \Phi_{CBODN}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \]

where:

  • \(\Theta\) = BOD temperature rate multiplier
  • \(T\) = temperature, °C
  • \(\omega_{CBOD}\) = CBOD settling velocity, m s⁻¹
  • \(K_{BOD}\) = CBOD decay rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_{CBODN}\) = CBODN concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Algae
docs.text: An algal community can be represented as a single assemblage or as multiple algae groups (Figure 88). Often, the algal groups might include diatoms, greens, and cyanobacteria. The user has complete freedom in how many and what kinds of algal groups can be included in the simulation through careful specification of the kinetic rate parameters that define the characteristics of each algal group.

docs.title: Source-Sink Term for Algae
docs.text:
Figure 88. Internal flux between algae and other compartments.

The rate equation for each algal group is:

\[ S_a = \underbrace{K_{ag}\Phi_a}_{\text{growth}} - \underbrace{K_{ar}\Phi_a}_{\text{respiration}} - \underbrace{K_{ae}\Phi_a}_{\text{excretion}} - \underbrace{K_{am}\Phi_a}_{\text{mortality}} - \underbrace{\omega_a\frac{1}{A}\frac{\partial A\Phi_a}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} - \underbrace{\sum\left(Z_\mu\Phi_{zoo}\frac{\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a}{\sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{lpom} + \sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo}}\right)}_{\text{net loss to grazing}} \tag{4-87} \]

where:

  • \(z\) = cell height
  • \(A\) = horizontal area
  • \(Z_\mu\) = net growth rate of a zooplankton species
  • \(\sigma_{alg}, \sigma_{zoo}\) = zooplankton grazing preference factors for algae (alg) or zooplankton (zoo)
  • \(K_{ag}\) = algal growth rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{ar}\) = algal dark respiration rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{ae}\) = algal excretion rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{am}\) = algal mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\omega_a\) = algal settling rate, m s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_a\) = algal concentration, g m⁻³

Chlorophyll a (chl a) is the most commonly available estimate of algal biomass. To convert chl a to algal biomass, multiply chl a by the ratio of algae (g m⁻³ dry weight organic matter) to chl a (µg L⁻¹).

docs.title: Algal Growth Rate
docs.text:
Algal growth rate is computed by modifying a maximum growth rate affected by temperature, light, and nutrient availability:

\[ K_{ag} = \gamma_{ar}\gamma_{af}\lambda_{\min}K_{ag\max} \tag{4-88} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{ar}\) = temperature rate multiplier for rising limb of curve
  • \(\gamma_{af}\) = temperature rate multiplier for falling limb of curve
  • \(\lambda_{\min}\) = multiplier for limiting growth factor (minimum of light, phosphorus, silica, and nitrogen) between 0 and 1
  • \(K_{ag}\) = algal growth rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{ag\max}\) = maximum algal growth rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: Light Limitation
docs.text:
The rate multiplier, \(\lambda_l\), between 0 and 1 for light is based upon the Steele (1962) function:

\[ \lambda_l = F(I) = \frac{I}{I_s}e^{-\frac{I}{I_s}+1} \tag{4-89} \]

where:

  • \(I\) = available light, W m⁻²
  • \(I_s\) = saturating light intensity at maximum photosynthetic rate, W m⁻²

The above expression allows for simulation of photoinhibition at light intensities greater than the saturation value. Light penetration decreases with depth:

\[ I(z) = (1-\beta)I_0 e^{-\alpha z} \tag{4-90} \]

where:

  • \(I_0\) = solar radiation at the water surface, W m⁻²
  • \(\alpha\) = attenuation coefficient, m⁻¹
  • \(z\) = depth, m
  • \((1-\beta)\) = fraction of solar radiation absorbed at the water surface

The average effect of light on algal growth in a particular model cell can be obtained by combining the above two expressions and integrating over the cell depth to obtain (Chapra and Reckhow, 1983):

\[ \lambda_l = \frac{e}{\alpha \Delta z}\left[e^{-\gamma_2} - e^{-\gamma_1}\right] \tag{4-91} \]

where:

\[ \gamma_1 = \frac{(1-\beta)I_0 e^{-\alpha d}}{I_s} \] \[ \gamma_2 = \frac{(1-\beta)I_0 e^{-\alpha(d+\Delta z)}}{I_s} \]

and \(d\) is the depth at the top of the model cell, m.

The fraction of solar radiation, \((1-\beta)I_0\), is added directly to the surface layer. The attenuation coefficient, \(\alpha\), consists of a baseline value [EXH2O] to which the effects of inorganic [EXINOR] and organic [EXORG] suspended solids, and algae [EXA] are added.

docs.title: Nutrient Limitation
docs.text:
Rate multipliers limiting maximum algal growth due to nutrient limitations are computed using the Monod relationship:

\[ \lambda_i = \frac{\Phi_i}{P_i + \Phi_i} \tag{4-92} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_i\) = phosphorus or nitrate + ammonium concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(P_i\) = half-saturation coefficient for phosphorus or nitrate + ammonium, g m⁻³

docs.title: Ammonium Preference
docs.text:
The algal nitrogen preference for ammonium is based upon the following (Thomann and Fitzpatrick, 1982) equation:

\[ P_{NH4} = \Phi_{NH4}\frac{\Phi_{NOx}}{(K_{NH4}+\Phi_{NH4})(K_{NH4}+\Phi_{NOx})} + \Phi_{NH4}\frac{K_{NH4}}{(\Phi_{NH4}+\Phi_{NOx})(K_{NH4}+\Phi_{NOx})} \tag{4-93} \]

where:

  • \(P_{NH4}\) = ammonium preference factor
  • \(K_{NH4}\) = ammonia preference half-saturation coefficient, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{NH4}\) = ammonium concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{NOx}\) = nitrate-nitrite concentration, g m⁻³

This allows algae to use primarily ammonium and gradually switch to nitrate as ammonium concentrations decrease.

docs.title: Algal Dark Respiration
docs.text:
Algal dark respiration is computed using the rising limb of the temperature function:

\[ K_{ar} = \gamma_{ar}\gamma_{af}K_{ar\max} \tag{4-94} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{ar}\) = temperature rate multiplier for rising limb of curve
  • \(\gamma_{af}\) = temperature rate multiplier for falling limb of curve
  • \(K_{ar\max}\) = maximum dark respiration rate, s⁻¹

docs.title: Algal Excretion
docs.text:
Algal photorespiration (excretion) is evaluated using an inverse relation to the light rate multiplier:

\[ K_{ae} = (1-\lambda_l)\gamma_{ar}\gamma_{af}K_{ae\max} \tag{4-95} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{ar}\) = temperature rate multiplier for rising limb of curve
  • \(\gamma_{af}\) = temperature rate multiplier for falling limb of curve
  • \(K_{ae\max}\) = maximum excretion rate constant, s⁻¹
  • \(\lambda_l\) = light limiting factor

Excretion rates increase at both low and high light intensities, with excretion products contributing to labile DOM.

docs.title: Algal Mortality
docs.text:
Algal mortality is defined as:

\[ K_{am} = \gamma_{ar}\gamma_{af}K_{am\max} \tag{4-96} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{ar}\) = temperature rate multiplier for rising limb of curve
  • \(\gamma_{af}\) = temperature rate multiplier for falling limb of curve
  • \(K_{am\max}\) = maximum mortality rate, s⁻¹

This mortality rate represents both natural and predator mortality. Algal growth does not occur in the absence of light. Algal growth is not allowed to exceed the limit imposed by nutrient supply over a given timestep. Algal excretion is not allowed to exceed algal growth rates.

Like inorganic solids, settling algae serve as a source for the layer below. Unlike inorganic solids, algae passing to the sediments accumulate within the sediment compartment. POM is also accumulated in this sediment compartment.

docs.title: Algae Vertical Migration
docs.text:
Some species of cyanobacteria, often responsible for harmful algal blooms (HABs), can move vertically in the water column through their own motility, independent of water velocity. This vertical migration can lead to HABs when colonies accumulate at the water surface and experience increased growth, degrading water quality and environmental health.

Cyanobacteria vertical migration is achieved through a process called buoyancy regulation. Cells regulate their buoyancy either with carbohydrate ballast or gas vesicles. Two different models were used to calculate a settling velocity for an algae group at each time step.

docs.title: Predefined Velocity
docs.text:
A simple way to model the vertical movement of cyanobacteria is to assume a velocity function for colonies based on knowledge of their typical movement. An equation for colony velocity as a function of time can be used:

\[ v_p(t) = A\frac{2\pi}{86{,}400\text{ s}}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{86{,}400\text{ s}}t + \phi\right) \]

where \(A\) is the migration amplitude and the period is assumed to be one day (86,400 seconds). The value of the phase (\(\phi\)) depends on the initial location of colonies.

The velocity function can also be dependent on space as well as time:

\[ v_p(t,z) = \begin{cases} A\frac{2\pi}{86{,}400\text{ s}}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{86{,}400\text{ s}}t + \phi\right)e^{-\alpha(H-z)}, & I_0 > 0 \\ A\frac{2\pi}{86{,}400\text{ s}}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{86{,}400\text{ s}}t + \phi\right), & I_0 \leq 0 \end{cases} \]

where \(\alpha\) is the light attenuation coefficient and \(I_0\) is solar irradiance at the water surface, \(H\) is a user-supplied depth parameter. The exponential term is only applied during the photoperiod.

docs.title: Dynamic Velocity
docs.text:
The predefined velocity approach can predict cyanobacteria movement based on the observed tendency of colonies to migrate vertically on a daily cycle; however, it does not reflect the response of colonies to variations in solar irradiance. The dynamic velocity model uses colony density computed based on solar irradiance:

\[ \frac{\partial \rho_c}{\partial t} = c_1 F(I) - c_2 \]

where \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are calibration coefficients. In the absence of light, density decreases at a constant rate. The numerical solution is:

\[ \rho_{c_i}^{n+1} = (c_1 F(I_i^n) - c_2)\Delta t + \rho_{c_i}^n \]

The function of light, \(F(I)\), must account for variations in light intensity over the depth of a model grid cell due to light attenuation with depth. The integral of light over the grid cell is (Chapra, 2008):

\[ F(I) = \frac{e}{\alpha \Delta z}[e^{-\gamma_2} - e^{-\gamma_1}] \]

where:

\[ \gamma_1 = \frac{(1-\beta)I_0}{I_s}e^{-\alpha(i-1)\Delta z} \qquad \gamma_2 = \frac{(1-\beta)I_0}{I_s}e^{-\alpha(i)\Delta z} \]

where \(\beta\) is the fraction of solar irradiance absorbed at the water surface and \(\alpha\) is the light attenuation coefficient (TVA, 1972). The height of the model grid cell is given by \(\Delta z\), \(I_0\) is irradiance at the water surface, and \(I_s\) is the saturating light intensity for the cyanobacteria species.

The settling velocity is then solved via Stokes' law:

\[ v = \frac{2gr^2(\rho_c - \rho')}{9\phi n} \]

where \(g\) is acceleration due to gravity, \(r\) is colony radius, \(\rho_c\) is cyanobacteria density, \(\rho'\) is density of water, \(\phi\) is form resistance, and \(n\) is viscosity of water.

An exponentially-decaying weighted average of past growth rates in each grid cell was applied:

\[ \rho_{c_i}^{n+1} = \frac{\sum_{q=-1}^{Q} \rho_{c_i}^{n-q} W^q}{\sum_{q=-1}^{Q} W^q} \]

where:

\[ W^q = e^{-k(t^{n+1}-t^{n-q})} \]

and \(k\) is the time decay constant for influence of past densities. This is similar to the approach taken by Serizawa et al. (2008).

In the dynamic velocity model, colonies were assumed to have a minimum and maximum allowable density (\(\rho_{min}\) and \(\rho_{max}\), respectively) as well as a constant radius based on values found in field studies (Table 13). When predicted densities were greater than the maximum or less than the minimum allowed values, the value was set to \(\rho_{max}\) or \(\rho_{min}\), respectively. It was also necessary to define initial densities (\(\rho_0\)) for all colonies within a grid cell. Initial colony density, \(\rho_{0_i}\), was assumed to vary exponentially from the surface to the bed, following a similar pattern to light decay with depth, as:

\[ \rho_{0_i} = \rho_{0_S} + (\rho_{0_B} - \rho_{0_S})(1 - e^{-z_i}) \]

where \(\rho_{0_S}\) is the initial colony density at the surface and \(\rho_{0_B}\) is the initial colony density at the bed.

docs.title: Algae Toxin Production
docs.text:
Cyanobacteria are known to produce toxins that can affect water quality in a surface waterbody. Not all genera or species produce toxins. The model considers both intracellular and extracellular toxins. The four main toxins modeled are microcystin (MC), cylindrospermopsin (CYN), anatoxin-a (ATX), and saxitoxin (STX).

Microcystin (MC) Cylindrospermopsin (CYN) Anatoxin-a (ATX) Saxitoxin (STX) Type Hepatotoxin (liver) Cytotoxin (several organs) Neurotoxin (nervous system) Neurotoxin (nervous system) Toxin Presence Mostly exist as intracellular toxins Mostly exist as extracellular toxins (dissolved) Highly water-soluble; extracellular mainly through cell lysis Paralytic shellfish toxins (accumulate in shellfish) Degradation Photodegradation (< 2 weeks); Biodegradation by bacteria Photodegradation (half-life of 20 days); UV (half-life of 18 hours) Biodegradation by bacteria (half-life of 5 days) Natural waters (half-life of 9-28 days)

Typical health guidelines for these toxins are shown in the following table.

Table 15. Oregon Health Authority Advisory Toxin Levels (Oregon Health Authority, 2020a, 2020b).

MC CYN ATX-a STX Units Notes OHA Recreational Use Values 4 8 8 4 µg L⁻¹ Everyone OHA Drinking Water Guidance Values 1.6 3 3 1.6 µg L⁻¹ Adults OHA Drinking Water Guidance Values 0.3 0.7 0.7 0.3 µg L⁻¹ Ages 5 years and younger

Notes:

  1. Units for STX are in saxitoxin equivalents: µg STX-eq L⁻¹.
  2. Advisory levels were provided for all four toxins in 2018, but only MC and CYN in drinking water are regulated under current rules.

The intracellular and extracellular toxin equations used in CE-QUAL-W2 are:

\[ C_{intra} = \sum_{i=1}^{n \text{ algal groups}} (CTP) \cdot \Phi_a \cdot \beta \tag{4-97} \] \[ \frac{dC_{extra}}{dt} = K_{am} \cdot \Phi_a \cdot \beta \cdot (CTP) + k_{release} \cdot C_{intra} - k_{decay} \cdot C_{extra} \tag{4-98} \]

where:

  • \(C_{intra}\) = intracellular toxin concentration
  • \(C_{extra}\) = extracellular toxin concentration
  • \(CTP\) = fraction of algae concentration producing toxin
  • \(\beta\) = ratio of intracellular toxin to dry weight biomass
  • \(k_{release}\) = toxin release rate
  • \(k_{decay}\) = extracellular decay rate

The intracellular toxin is calculated based only on the concentration of algae present in a model cell and the fraction of algae producing that toxin. The intracellular concentration is summed for all the algal groups that produce that toxin. There are no decay or other rates associated with the intracellular toxin concentration. The extracellular rate equation is only a function of the death rate of algae, the release rate of intracellular toxin, and the extracellular decay. Only one value is allowed for the release rate and decay rate for each toxin being modeled.

Each of the four toxins (microcystin, cylindrospermopsin, anatoxin-a, and saxitoxin) have been added as state variables to the CE-QUAL-W2 code with the option to turn any of them "on" or "off" depending on the cyanobacteria species that grow in the waterbody of interest.

docs.title: Periphyton/Epiphyton
docs.text:
Any number of user-defined periphyton/epiphyton groups can be modeled (Figure 90). Similar to the first-order sediment compartment, periphyton/epiphyton are not transported in the water column.

Figure 90. Internal flux between epiphyton and other compartments.

The rate equation for each epiphyton/periphyton group is:

\[ S_e = \underbrace{K_{eg}\Phi_e}_{\text{growth}} - \underbrace{K_{er}\Phi_e}_{\text{respiration}} - \underbrace{K_{ee}\Phi_e}_{\text{excretion}} - \underbrace{K_{em}\Phi_e}_{\text{mortality}} - \underbrace{K_{eb}\Phi_e}_{\text{burial}} \tag{4-99} \]

where:

  • \(K_{eg}\) = epiphyton growth rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{er}\) = epiphyton dark respiration rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{ee}\) = epiphyton excretion rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{em}\) = epiphyton mortality rate, s⁻¹
  • \(K_{eb}\) = epiphyton burial rate, s⁻¹
  • \(\Phi_e\) = epiphyton concentration, g m⁻³

docs.title: Epiphyton Growth Rate
docs.text:
Epiphyton/periphyton growth rate is computed by modifying a maximum growth rate affected by epiphyton/periphyton biomass, temperature, and nutrient availability:

\[ K_{eg} = \gamma_{er}\gamma_{ef}\lambda_{\min}K_{eg\max} \tag{4-100} \]

where:

  • \(\gamma_{er}\) = temperature rate multiplier for rising limb of curve
  • \(\gamma_{ef}\) = temperature rate multiplier for falling limb of curve
  • \(\lambda_{\min}\) = multiplier for limiting growth factor (minimum of phosphorus, silica, nitrogen, and epiphyton/periphyton biomass) between 0 and 1
  • \(K_{eg\max}\) = maximum epiphyton/periphyton growth rate, s⁻¹

The rate multiplier for light is based upon the Steele (1962) function:

\[ \lambda_l = F(I) = \frac{I}{I_s}e^{-\frac{I}{I_s}+1} \tag{4-101} \]

Light penetration decreases with depth:

\[ I(z) = (1-\beta)I_0 e^{-\alpha z} \tag{4-102} \]

The average effect of light on epiphyton/periphyton growth in a model cell is:

\[ \lambda_l = \frac{e}{\alpha \Delta z}\left[e^{-\gamma_2} - e^{-\gamma_1}\right] \tag{4-103} \]

The attenuation coefficient, \(\alpha\), is computed from a baseline value [EXH2O] to which the effects of inorganic [EXINOR] and organic [EXORG] suspended solids, as well as the extinction of each algal group, are added. Epiphyton/periphyton self-shading is accounted for in the biomass limitation formulation.

Nutrient limitation uses the Monod relationship:

\[ \lambda_i = \frac{\Phi_i}{P_i + \Phi_i} \tag{4-104} \]

The epiphyton/periphyton preference for ammonium is modeled using (Thomann and Fitzpatrick, 1982):

\[ P_{NH4} = \Phi_{NH4}\frac{\Phi_{NOx}}{(K_{NH4}+\Phi_{NH4})(K_{NH4}+\Phi_{NOx})} + \Phi_{NH4}\frac{K_{NH4}}{(\Phi_{NH4}+\Phi_{NOx})(K_{NH4}+\Phi_{NOx})} \tag{4-105} \]

docs.title: Epiphyton Respiration, Excretion, Mortality
docs.text:
Epiphyton/periphyton dark respiration:

\[ K_{er} = \gamma_{er}\gamma_{ef}K_{er\max} \tag{4-106} \]

Epiphyton/periphyton excretion:

\[ K_{ee} = (1-\lambda_l)\gamma_{er}\gamma_{ef}K_{ee\max} \tag{4-107} \]

Epiphyton/periphyton mortality:

\[ K_{em} = \gamma_{er}\gamma_{ef}K_{em\max} \tag{4-108} \]

Epiphyton/periphyton that die (mortality) become a part of the labile particulate organic matter and the labile dissolved organic matter pool. The user defines the fraction of the dead epiphyton (EPOM) that goes to the LPOM pool. The epiphyton/periphyton burial rate represents the burial of dead epiphyton/periphyton to the organic sediment compartment and becomes part of the first-order sediment compartment.

docs.title: Biomass Limitation
docs.text:
The epiphyton/periphyton biomass is controlled by a biomass limitation equation based on Monod kinetics. The biomass limitation function, \(f\) [BLIM], varies from 0 to 1 and is multiplied with the growth rate:

\[ f = \left[1 - \frac{B}{B + K_B}\right] \tag{4-109} \]

where:

  • \(B\) = epiphyton areal biomass, g m⁻² [EPD]
  • \(K_B\) = epiphyton areal biomass half-saturation coefficient, g m⁻² [EHS]

The areal biomass is calculated as:

\[ B = \Phi_e \frac{V}{A} \tag{4-110} \]

where:

  • \(A\) = computational cell surface area including side walls and bottom area, m²
  • \(V\) = computational cell volume, m³
  • \(\Phi_e\) = epiphyton concentration, g m⁻³

The biomass limitation is a surrogate calibration parameter for light limitation due to self-shading.

docs.title: Macrophytes
docs.text:
The macrophyte model consists of two parts: a section describing the water quality compartment and a section describing the hydrodynamic compartment. Both sections are from Berger (2000) and Berger and Wells (2008).

The macrophyte model simulates multiple submerged macrophyte species without differentiating between plant parts (Figure 92). Light, temperature, carbon dioxide, ammonia-nitrogen (the sole nitrogen source for macrophytes), and ortho-phosphorus may limit growth. Depending on the macrophyte species, nitrogen and phosphorus may be obtained from the sediments or the water column. Plants grow upward from the sediment through model layers. Macrophyte shading is modeled by making light attenuation a function of macrophyte concentration.

Figure 92. Nutrient fluxes for the macrophyte compartment in CE-QUAL-W2.

The macrophyte growth rate is modeled as:

\[ S_{macro} = \underbrace{\mu_{m\max}f(I,N,P,C)\gamma_1\gamma_2\Phi_{macro}}_{\text{growth}} - \underbrace{K_{mr}\gamma_1\Phi_{macro}}_{\text{respiration}} - \underbrace{K_{mm}\Phi_{macro}}_{\text{mortality}} \tag{4-111} \]

where:

  • \(S_{macro}\) = macrophyte growth rate density, g m⁻³ s⁻¹
  • \(I\) = solar radiation, W m⁻²
  • \(f(I,N,P,C)\) = growth limiting function between 0 and 1
  • \(\mu_{m\max}\) = maximum macrophyte growth rate (input: d⁻¹; internal: s⁻¹)
  • \(K_{mr}\) = maximum respiration rate (input: d⁻¹; internal: s⁻¹)
  • \(K_{mm}\) = mortality/excretion rate (input: d⁻¹; internal: s⁻¹)
  • \(\gamma_1\) = ascending temperature rate multiplier
  • \(\gamma_2\) = descending temperature rate multiplier
  • \(\Phi_{macro}\) = macrophyte concentration, g m⁻³

Growth rate, respiration rate, and mortality/excretion rate are temperature dependent. Temperature effects are modeled using the equations developed by Thornton and Lessem (1978), also used in the phytoplankton compartment of CE-QUAL-W2. The growth limiting function \(f(I,N,P,C)\) is the minimum of the light \(f(I)\), nitrogen \(f(N)\), phosphorus \(f(P)\), and carbon \(f(C)\) limiting functions:

\[ f(I,N,P,C) = \min(f(I), f(N), f(P), f(C)) \]

All the limiting functions are unitless and have a value between 0 and 1. The limiting functions for the nutrients have the Michaelis-Menten form:

\[ f(S) = \frac{S}{K_S + S} \tag{4-112} \]

where \(S\) is the nutrient concentration (g m⁻³) and \(K_S\) is the half-saturation concentration (g m⁻³).

Light limitation is modeled with a hyperbolic equation:

\[ f(I) = \frac{I}{I + I_h} \tag{4-113} \]

where \(I\) is solar radiation (W m⁻²) and \(I_h\) is the half-saturation coefficient for solar radiation (W m⁻²). This function is frequently used in the absence of photoinhibition.

The net light extinction coefficient (m⁻¹) is modeled as a function of macrophyte plant tissue concentration:

\[ \gamma = \varepsilon_{H_2O} + \varepsilon_{iss}\Phi_{iss} + \varepsilon_{oss}\Phi_{oss} + \sum_{\substack{\text{macrophyte} \\ \text{groups}}} \varepsilon_{mac}\Phi_{mac} + \sum_{\substack{\text{algae} \\ \text{groups}}} \varepsilon_{algae}\Phi_{algae} \tag{4-114} \]

where:

  • \(\varepsilon_{H_2O}\) = light extinction exclusive of suspended solids, m⁻¹ [EXH2O]
  • \(\varepsilon_{iss}\) = light extinction due to inorganic suspended solids, m² g⁻¹ [EXINOR]
  • \(\varepsilon_{oss}\) = light extinction due to non-living organic suspended solids, m² g⁻¹ [EXORG]
  • \(\varepsilon_{mac}\) = light extinction due to macrophytes, m² g⁻¹ [EXM]
  • \(\varepsilon_{algae}\) = light extinction due to algae, m² g⁻¹ [EXA]

docs.title: Modeling Frictional Force
docs.text:
Modeling of flow through macrophytes incorporates the following concepts:

  • Porosity of the macrophytes was calculated through determination of the blockage area of the vegetation normal to the direction of flow
  • The drag of individual stems and leaves were totaled to determine the total drag force in a model cell
  • The effective Manning's \(n\) was calculated by combining the effect of bed shear and the drag force on the plants

The total frictional force \(f\) was partitioned into a bottom friction component \(f_b\) and a vegetation drag component \(f_v\):

\[ f = f_b + f_v \tag{4-115} \]

Bottom shear \(\tau_b\) was simulated using Manning's friction factor:

\[ \tau_b = \frac{\rho_w g n^2}{R^{1/3}} U|U| \tag{4-116} \]

The effective Manning's \(n\) of each model cell was calculated in the manner used by Petryk and Bosmajian (1975):

\[ n = n_b\sqrt{1 + \frac{C_d \sum A_i}{2gAL}\frac{1}{n_b^2}R^{4/3}} \tag{4-117} \]

where \(n_b\) is the Manning's friction factor due to bed shear only.

docs.title: Modeling Porosity
docs.text:
The volume \(V_m\) of macrophytes can be estimated by dividing the macrophyte mass in a model cell \(m\) by density \(\rho_m\):

\[ V_m = \frac{m}{\rho_m} \]

The porosity \(\varphi\) was estimated by dividing volume within a cell free of macrophytes by the cell total volume \(V\):

\[ \varphi = \left(\frac{V - V_m}{V}\right) \]

docs.title: Changes to Governing Equations
docs.text:
Several of the governing equations have been altered to account for porosity and the frictional effects of macrophytes. The new x-momentum equation is:

\[ \frac{\partial U\varphi B}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial UU\varphi B}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial WU\varphi B}{\partial z} = -\frac{\varphi B}{\rho}\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial \varphi B\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial \varphi B\tau_{xz}}{\partial z} \tag{4-118} \]

where \(U\) is x-direction velocity (m/sec), \(W\) is z-direction velocity (m/sec), \(B\) is channel width (m), \(\rho\) is density (kg m⁻³), \(P\) is pressure (N m⁻²), \(\tau_{xz}\) is vertical shear stress (N m⁻²), \(\tau_{xx}\) is longitudinal shear stress (N m⁻²), and \(\varphi\) is porosity.

Vertical shear stress \(\tau_{xz}\) is a function of interfacial shear stress, shear stress due to wind, and bottom and plant shear stress. It was determined from:

\[ \frac{\tau_{xz}}{\rho} = A_z\frac{\partial U}{\partial z} + \frac{\tau_{wx}}{\rho}e^{-dkz} + \frac{\tau_{bm}}{\rho} \tag{4-119} \]

where \(\tau_{bm}\) is bottom and plant shear stress, \(A_z\) is turbulent eddy viscosity, \(\tau_{wx}\) is wind shear stress, and \(k\) is wave number.

Bottom and plant shear stress is calculated using the effective Manning's \(n\) determined above:

\[ \tau_{bm} = \frac{\rho g n^2}{R^{1/3}}U|U| \tag{4-120} \]

The continuity equation was changed to:

\[ \frac{\partial U\varphi B}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial W\varphi B}{\partial z} = q\varphi B \tag{4-121} \]

The new free water surface equation is:

\[ \frac{\partial B_\eta \varphi \eta}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\int_\eta^h U\varphi B dz - \int_\eta^h q\varphi B dz \tag{4-122} \]

The constituent transport equation was modified to:

\[ \frac{\partial \varphi BC}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial U\varphi BC}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial W\varphi BC}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\varphi BD_x\frac{\partial C}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\varphi BD_z\frac{\partial C}{\partial z} = q_\varphi\varphi B + S_K\varphi B \tag{4-123} \]

docs.title: Zooplankton
docs.text:
The zooplankton compartment (Figure 93) was adapted from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) reservoir model CE-QUAL-R1 (Environmental Laboratory, 1995). Zooplankton are assumed to be non-motile and are transported only by advection and dispersion. Zooplankton can graze algae, detritus (POM), and other zooplankton. Losses occur through mortality and respiration. Algae vertical settling or floating can also be specified through a settling velocity and dynamic vertical migration.

Figure 93. Zooplankton source/sinks.

The source/sink term for zooplankton is:

\[ S_{zoo} = \underbrace{\gamma_1\gamma_2 Z_e K_{z\max}\left(\frac{(\sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{lpom} + \sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo}) - Z_L}{(\sum\sigma_{alg}\Phi_a + \sigma_{pom}\Phi_{lpom} + \sum\sigma_{zoo}\Phi_{zoo}) + Z_{1/2}}\right)\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{growth}} \] \[ - \underbrace{(1-\gamma_2)K_{zm}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{mortality}} - \underbrace{\gamma_1 K_{zr}\Phi_{zoo}}_{\text{respiration}} - \underbrace{\omega_{zoo}\frac{\partial \Phi_{zoo}}{\partial z}}_{\text{settling}} \]

where:

  • \(\Phi_{lpom}\) = labile particulate organic matter concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_a\) = algae concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(\Phi_{zoo}\) = zooplankton concentration, g m⁻³
  • \(K_{zm}\) = zooplankton mortality rate (input: d⁻¹; internal: s⁻¹)
  • \(K_{z\max}\) = maximum ingestion rate for zooplankton (input: d⁻¹; internal: s⁻¹)
  • \(K_{zr}\) = zooplankton respiration rate (input: d⁻¹; internal: s⁻¹)
  • \(Z_{1/2}\) = half-saturation coefficient for zooplankton ingestion, g m⁻³
  • \(Z_e\) = zooplankton ingestion efficiency
  • \(Z_L\) = low threshold concentration for zooplankton feeding, g m⁻³
  • \(\gamma_1\) = temperature coefficient for rising limb of curve for zooplankton
  • \(\gamma_2\) = temperature coefficient for falling limb of curve for zooplankton
  • \(\sigma_{alg}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for algae
  • \(\sigma_{zoo}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for zooplankton
  • \(\sigma_{pom}\) = zooplankton preference fraction for particulate organic matter
  • \(\omega_{zoo}\) = zooplankton settling velocity

The growth rate is a function of temperature, the maximum growth rate, and a modified Michaelis-Menten equation that includes a low threshold concentration below which zooplankton do not feed. At dissolved oxygen concentrations below 2 g m⁻³, feeding stops and the mortality rate is doubled.
